metadata.title: Head injury: assessment and early management
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the assessment and early management of head injury in babies, children, young people and adults. It covers pre-hospital referral, emergency assessment, imaging, early treatment, admission, transfer to specialist care, discharge and follow up. Its aim is to match care to injury severity and enable direct referral to specialist services when needed.

conditions_covered: isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture
care_settings: inpatient units without an emergency department
target_population: children and young people aged 1 year to under 16 years
people 16 and over with a head injury
therapeutic_areas: CT imaging of the head and cervical spine

therapies_index.name: tranexamic acid
approved_indications: Consider for people with a head injury and a GCS score of 12 or less when active extracranial bleeding is not suspected.
therapies_index.administration: Give an intravenous bolus as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury, before imaging, either before arrival at hospital or in hospital: 2 g for people 16 and over; 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 2 g) for people under 16. These uses were off-label in March 2023.
key_toxicities: For mild traumatic brain injury, whether potential benefit outweighs the possible risk of blood clots is uncertain.

therapies_index.name: prothrombin complex concentrate
approved_indications: The guideline refers elsewhere for advice about reversing vitamin K antagonists in people with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage.

therapies_index.name: vasopressors
approved_indications: Use when indicated to maintain mean arterial pressure in an intubated person being transferred to a neuroscience unit.
therapies_index.administration: Infuse as indicated, together with fluid, to maintain mean arterial pressure at 80 mmHg or more.

therapies_index.name: fluid
approved_indications: Use when indicated to support mean arterial pressure in an intubated person being transferred to a neuroscience unit.
therapies_index.administration: Infuse as indicated, together with vasopressors, to maintain mean arterial pressure at 80 mmHg or more.

therapies_index.name: oxygen
approved_indications: Use during ventilation of people being transferred to a neuroscience unit.
therapies_index.administration: For intubated people 16 and over, aim for a PaO2 of more than 13 kPa; increase inspired oxygen concentration if hyperventilation is used. For people under 16, ventilate according to the oxygen saturation level appropriate for their age.
monitoring: Age-appropriate oxygen saturation in people under 16.

therapies_index.name: sedation
approved_indications: Provide to a person whose trachea is intubated.
therapies_index.administration: Use with appropriate analgesia and a neuromuscular blocking drug.

therapies_index.name: analgesia
approved_indications: Treat pain effectively in people with a head injury to help prevent a rise in intracranial pressure.
Provide to a person whose trachea is intubated.
therapies_index.administration: For an intubated person, use with appropriate sedation and a neuromuscular blocking drug.

therapies_index.name: neuromuscular blocking drug
approved_indications: Provide to a person whose trachea is intubated.
therapies_index.administration: Use with appropriate sedation and analgesia.

therapies_index.name: CT head scan
approved_indications: CT of the head is the primary investigation for detecting acute clinically important traumatic brain injury.
In people 16 and over, perform within 1 hour after identifying any risk factor specified in recommendation 1.5.8.

In people 16 and over with loss of consciousness or amnesia, perform within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour if presentation is more than 8 hours after injury, when a risk factor in recommendation 1.5.9 is present.
In people under 16, perform within 1 hour when a risk factor in recommendation 1.5.10 is identified, or when more than 1 risk factor in recommendation 1.5.11 is present.
In people under 16 initially observed because they have only 1 risk factor in recommendation 1.5.11, perform within 1 hour if the specified deterioration occurs.
Consider for people taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment, excluding aspirin monotherapy, who have no other indication for a CT head scan.
Consider an immediate scan when neurological deterioration during hospital observation is confirmed.
therapies_index.administration: For the medication-only consideration, consider scanning within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour if presentation is more than 8 hours after injury.
monitoring: Make a provisional written radiology report available within 1 hour of the scan.
Minimise radiation dose while maintaining sufficient diagnostic image quality and coverage.

therapies_index.name: CT cervical spine scan
approved_indications: For people 16 and over with a head injury, perform within 1 hour when a high-risk factor in recommendation 1.6.2 is identified.
For people 16 and over with neck pain or tenderness but no high-risk indication, perform within 1 hour when a factor in recommendation 1.6.3 applies.
For people under 16 with a head injury, perform only when a factor in recommendation 1.6.4 applies, within 1 hour of its identification.
monitoring: Base the report on high-resolution source data and multiplanar reformatting covering the entire cervical spine.
Make a provisional written radiology report available within 1 hour of the scan.
Minimise radiation dose while maintaining sufficient diagnostic image quality and coverage.

therapies_index.name: MRI
approved_indications: MRI is not recommended as the primary investigation of clinically important traumatic brain injury, although it can sometimes provide additional prognostic information.
Perform in addition to CT if neurological signs and symptoms suggest cervical spine injury.
Consider for ligamentous or disc injuries suggested by CT or clinical findings.
Consider a further MRI or CT scan, after discussion with radiology, when a person still does not have a GCS score of 15 after 24 hours of observation despite a normal CT scan.
monitoring: Have suitable monitoring equipment available for a person with a head injury undergoing MRI.
Ensure staff know the hazards and required precautions near the MRI scanner.

therapies_index.name: 3-view cervical spine X-rays
approved_indications: For people under 16 with a head injury and neck pain or tenderness but no indication for CT cervical spine scanning, obtain before neck movement assessment when a factor in recommendation 1.6.5 applies.

For people under 16 whose neck movement can be assessed safely and who have neck pain or tenderness but no CT indication, obtain if they cannot actively rotate their neck 45 degrees to the left and right.
therapies_index.administration: Obtain within 1 hour after identifying the relevant risk factor. A peg view may be omitted when the person cannot understand commands or open their mouth.
monitoring: Have a clinician trained in interpretation review the X-rays.

therapies_index.name: plain X-rays of the skull
approved_indications: Do not use to diagnose important traumatic brain injury before discussion with a neuroscience unit.

therapies_index.name: skeletal survey
approved_indications: May be needed for a person under 16 with suspected non-accidental injury.

therapies_index.name: CT or MRI angiography of the neck vessels
approved_indications: Perform when vascular injury is suspected, including suspicion arising from vertebral malalignment, a high-risk fracture or posterior circulation syndrome.

therapies_index.name: intubation and ventilation
approved_indications: Use for anyone with a GCS score of 8 or less who needs transfer to a neuroscience unit.
Intubate and ventilate immediately for coma, absent protective laryngeal reflexes, ventilatory insufficiency or irregular respirations.
Use before transfer when consciousness is deteriorating significantly, facial skeletal fractures are unstable, there is copious oral bleeding or seizures occur.
Apply the transfer principles to people under 16, using the paediatric GCS modification for preverbal and non-verbal children.
therapies_index.administration: For intubated people 16 and over, aim for a PaO2 of more than 13 kPa and a PaCO2 of 4.5 kPa to 5.0 kPa, unless clinical or radiological evidence of raised intracranial pressure justifies more aggressive hyperventilation. If hyperventilation is used, increase inspired oxygen concentration. For people under 16, ventilate according to age-appropriate oxygen saturation.
monitoring: Assess blood gases when judging ventilatory insufficiency: hypoxaemia is PaO2 less than 13 kPa on oxygen and hypercarbia is PaCO2 more than 6 kPa.
Monitor PaO2 and PaCO2 in intubated people 16 and over.
Monitor age-appropriate oxygen saturation in people under 16.

therapies_index.name: full in-line spine immobilisation
approved_indications: The guideline refers elsewhere for criteria and duration when immobilisation is indicated.

therapies_index.name: splint limb fractures
approved_indications: Use when needed as part of immediate or emergency-department care for a person with a head injury.

therapies_index.name: catheterise a full bladder
approved_indications: Use when needed as part of immediate or emergency-department care for a person with a head injury.

therapies_index.name: transfer to a neuroscience unit
approved_indications: Transfer can benefit anyone with a serious head injury and a GCS score of 8 or less, whether or not neurosurgery is required.
When transfer of someone who does not need neurosurgery is not possible, maintain clinical liaison with the neuroscience unit.
therapies_index.administration: Complete initial resuscitation and stabilisation and establish comprehensive monitoring before transfer. Do not transport a person with persistent hypotension despite resuscitation until its cause has been identified and the person is stable.
monitoring: Provide the transfer team with a way to communicate changes in the person's condition during the journey.

therapies_index.name: in-hospital observation
approved_indications: Observe people admitted after a head injury using staff competent in head injury assessment.
For a person under 16 with only 1 risk factor in recommendation 1.5.11, observe for a minimum of 4 hours from the time of injury.
Observation of babies and children under 5 should take place only in units with staff experienced in observing this age group after head injury.
therapies_index.administration: For admitted people, record observations half-hourly until the GCS score is 15. Once the GCS score is 15, observe half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly; return to half-hourly observations and repeat the original schedule if deterioration occurs after the initial 2-hour period.
monitoring: Document GCS score, pupil size and reactivity, limb movements, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and blood oxygen saturation.
Urgently reassess signs of neurological deterioration.

conditions.name: head injury
conditions.description: Trauma affecting the head, excluding superficial facial injuries; the definition encompasses closed and penetrating injuries.
conditions.epidemiology: In the UK, head injuries are a major cause of death and disability among people aged 1 to 40. Each year, over 1 million people attend emergency departments in England and Wales after a recent head injury; between 33% and 50% are aged under 15. About 200,000 people are admitted annually, including about 40,000 with evidence of traumatic brain injury. As few as 0.2% of emergency department attendees die because of the injury. Among people with a head injury, 95% present with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 13 or more; those with moderate or severe injury account for only 5% of attendees but experience most fatal outcomes. An increasing proportion of attendees are over 65. Abuse is estimated to cause head injury in 25% to 30% of hospitalised children under 2.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible findings include altered consciousness, amnesia, headache, vomiting, seizure, focal neurological deficits and signs of skull fracture. Irritability or a change in behaviour can be particularly relevant in babies and children under 5. Some people subsequently experience persistent physical, cognitive, emotional or hormonal problems.

subtypes.name: Closed head injury
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An impact or indirect force injures the head without an object penetrating the skull or brain.

subtypes.name: Penetrating head injury
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An object passes through the scalp and skull into the brain or its lining.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess consciousness and the severity of associated traumatic brain injury, and monitor for deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use during initial assessment and ongoing observation; establish the pre-injury baseline where possible if it may be less than 15.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Record eye-opening, verbal and motor responses separately alongside a total out of 15. Use the paediatric version, including a grimace alternative to the verbal response, for preverbal children.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify an acute clinically important traumatic brain injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For people 16 and over, perform within 1 hour after identifying an initial emergency department GCS score of 12 or less, a GCS score below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, a sign of basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit or more than 1 vomiting episode. After loss of consciousness or amnesia, perform within 8 hours of injury if the person is aged 65 or over, has a current bleeding or clotting disorder, experienced the specified dangerous mechanism or has more than 30 minutes' retrograde amnesia; perform within the hour if they present more than 8 hours after injury.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture is unlikely to be a clinically important imaging abnormality unless the person takes anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify an acute clinically important traumatic brain injury in people under 16.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform within 1 hour for suspected non-accidental injury, post-traumatic seizure, an initial GCS score below 14 or a paediatric GCS score below 15 in babies under 1 year, a GCS score below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture or tense fontanelle, a sign of basal skull fracture, focal neurological deficit, or a head bruise, swelling or laceration exceeding 5 cm in babies under 1 year. Also perform within 1 hour if more than 1 of these factors is present: witnessed loss of consciousness lasting more than 5 minutes, abnormal drowsiness, 3 or more separate vomiting episodes, the specified dangerous mechanism, amnesia lasting more than 5 minutes or a current bleeding or clotting disorder.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If only 1 factor from the second group is present, observe for a minimum of 4 hours from injury. Obtain CT within 1 hour if GCS becomes less than 15, vomiting recurs or another episode of abnormal drowsiness occurs. If none occurs, use clinical judgement about longer observation. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for intracranial injury in people taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication who have no other indication for head CT.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider within 8 hours of injury for people receiving anticoagulants or antiplatelets other than aspirin monotherapy, or within the hour if presentation is more than 8 hours after injury.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The decision to scan is conditional rather than automatic; consider the ability to assess risk and whether the person would return if deterioration developed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional information that can sometimes be relevant to prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be used as an additional investigation; it is not the primary investigation for clinically important traumatic brain injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated for prediction of acute complications or post-concussion syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The committee found insufficient evidence to recommend their use for these predictive purposes.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The 3 responses are scored independently and summed to a total from 3 to 15. A person's pre-injury baseline may be less than 15.

follow_up.schedule: A responsible adult should remain with the person for the first 24 hours after injury. Send the GP details of the emergency department history and examination within 48 hours of discharge.
recommended_tests: Consider a further CT or MRI scan, in discussion with radiology, if the initial CT was normal but GCS has not reached 15 after 24 hours of observation.
Consider endocrinology investigations after discharge if symptoms suggest hypopituitarism or recovery is not as expected.
long_term_effects: Persistent or delayed physical, sensory, motor, cognitive and emotional problems
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Provide verbal and age-appropriate printed discharge information about deterioration, delayed symptoms, recovery, support services and return to everyday activities. Consider referral to a clinician experienced in the consequences of traumatic brain injury for persisting problems, and investigate injury causes or contributing factors when appropriate.

conditions.name: Closed head injury
conditions.description: A direct blow or an indirect force, such as shaking or deceleration, causes injury without an object entering the skull or brain. Injury may involve stretching or tearing of nerves at the brain base, blood clots in or around the brain, or brain swelling. A skull fracture may occur without creating a direct connection between the brain and the exterior.

conditions.name: Penetrating head injury
conditions.description: An object enters through the scalp and skull and reaches the brain or its lining.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Penetration may be apparent on examination; a cerebrospinal fluid leak or other signs of a complex skull injury may raise concern.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a suspected penetrating injury and associated intracranial injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: A suspected penetrating head injury requires urgent hospital assessment; discuss a definite or suspected penetrating injury with a neurosurgeon regardless of imaging findings.

conditions.name: Traumatic brain injury
conditions.description: An external force causes a change in brain function or other evidence of brain pathology.
conditions.epidemiology: Among about 200,000 people admitted to hospital each year with a head injury, about 40,000 have evidence of traumatic brain injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Consciousness may be impaired, and neurological deficits, confusion, seizures or deterioration can occur. Persistent physical, sensory, motor, cognitive, emotional and hormonal problems are possible even after normal initial imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Serve as the primary investigation for an acute clinically important traumatic brain injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Apply the age-specific CT head criteria for head injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Sometimes identify further information relevant to prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May supplement assessment but should not be the primary investigation for clinically important traumatic brain injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess severity and detect changes in neurological function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At assessment and during observation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A total of 13 to 15 denotes mild, 9 to 12 moderate, and 8 or less severe traumatic brain injury; document the individual responses as well as the total.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated as predictors of acute complications.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The evidence did not support a recommendation to use these tests to predict acute complications after mild traumatic brain injury.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The total ranges from 3, indicating no response in any domain, to 15, indicating no response deficit. Consider a baseline below 15 when present before injury.

recommended_tests: Consider investigations for hypopituitarism when indicated by persistent symptoms or findings.
long_term_effects: Persistent physical, sensory, motor, cognitive and emotional difficulties
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Consider referral for persisting problems to a clinician trained in assessing and managing the consequences of traumatic brain injury.

conditions.name: Mild traumatic brain injury
conditions.description: Traumatic brain injury classified by a GCS score of 13 to 15.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Problems may persist despite a normal or minimally impaired level of consciousness; post-concussion symptoms may be under-recognised.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the injury's severity category.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment and observation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A GCS score of 13 to 15 falls in the mild traumatic brain injury category.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a clinically important intracranial injury when head injury risk criteria indicate imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use the age-specific head injury criteria rather than mild severity alone.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated for prediction of acute complications or post-concussion syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The committee found the evidence too limited to recommend these predictive uses.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated for prediction of post-concussion syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The evidence was too limited to recommend MRI for this predictive purpose.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Document each component with the total score.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Explain the possibility of persistent or delayed symptoms and consider specialist referral if problems persist.

conditions.name: Moderate traumatic brain injury
conditions.description: Traumatic brain injury classified by a GCS score of 9 to 12.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Impaired consciousness is reflected in the GCS severity category.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Classify injury severity and monitor neurological status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During initial assessment and subsequent observation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A GCS score of 9 to 12 denotes moderate traumatic brain injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect acute clinically important traumatic brain injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For people 16 and over, an initial emergency department GCS score of 12 or less calls for CT within 1 hour. Apply the separate criteria for people under 16.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Record the components separately alongside the total.

conditions.name: Severe traumatic brain injury
conditions.description: Traumatic brain injury classified by a GCS score of 8 or less.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Severely reduced consciousness may include coma. Deterioration, abnormal breathing or loss of protective laryngeal reflexes may require immediate airway intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify severe injury and monitor neurological deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment, resuscitation and observation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A GCS score of 8 or less denotes severe traumatic brain injury and is a criterion for early involvement of a clinician trained in advanced airway management.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify acute intracranial abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Apply the age-specific urgent head CT criteria.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Record the individual components as well as the total; the paediatric modification applies to preverbal and non-verbal children.

conditions.name: cervical spine injury
conditions.description: Injury to the cervical spine considered during assessment of a person with a head injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Neck pain or tenderness, focal peripheral neurological signs and paraesthesia may raise suspicion; neurological findings can also suggest injury despite other imaging.

diagnostic_workup.test: range of movement in the neck
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether active neck rotation is preserved.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before imaging, assess only when no high-risk factors are present and at least 1 specified low-risk feature applies: a simple rear-end motor vehicle collision, comfortable sitting, walking at any time since injury, no midline cervical tenderness or delayed neck pain.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Inability to rotate actively 45 degrees to both the left and right is an imaging criterion in the specified groups.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected cervical spine injury in people 16 and over.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform within 1 hour for an initial GCS score of 12 or less, intubation, an urgent need for a definitive diagnosis, blunt polytrauma involving the head and chest, abdomen or pelvis in an alert and stable person, or suspected cervical spine injury accompanied by age 65 or over, the specified dangerous mechanism, focal peripheral neurological deficit or limb paraesthesia. With neck pain or tenderness but no high-risk indication, perform within 1 hour if movement assessment is unsafe, active rotation is less than 45 degrees in either direction, or a condition predisposes to cervical spine injury.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reports should use high-resolution source data and multiplanar reformats covering the entire cervical spine.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate cervical spine injury in people under 16.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform only for an initial GCS score of 12 or less, intubation, focal peripheral neurological signs, limb paraesthesia, an urgent need for a definitive diagnosis, other body imaging for head injury or multisystem trauma with clinical suspicion of cervical injury, strong suspicion despite normal X-rays, technically difficult or inadequate X-rays, or a significant bony injury on plain X-rays. Perform within 1 hour after identifying the factor.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate people under 16 with neck pain or tenderness but no indication for cervical CT.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain before neck movement assessment when there was the specified dangerous mechanism, safe movement assessment is impossible, or a predisposing condition is present. Also obtain if safe assessment shows inability to rotate actively 45 degrees to the left and right. Complete within 1 hour of identifying the factor.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A clinician trained in interpreting the images should review them. A peg view may be omitted if the person cannot understand commands or open their mouth.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further investigate neurological findings or possible ligamentous and disc injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform in addition to CT for neurological signs and symptoms suggesting cervical spine injury; consider it for ligamentous or disc injury suggested clinically or by CT.

diagnostic_workup.test: CT or MRI angiography of the neck vessels
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible vascular injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use when vascular injury is suspected, such as with vertebral malalignment, a specified high-risk fracture or posterior circulation syndrome.

long_term_effects: Disability can result if an important cervical spine injury is missed.

conditions.name: Isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture
conditions.description: A solitary linear skull fracture without inward or outward displacement, multiple fracture lines, or involvement or crossing of normal skull sutures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and characterise skull and intracranial abnormalities when head injury imaging criteria are met.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Apply the age-specific head CT criteria.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An isolated simple linear non-displaced fracture is unlikely to represent a clinically important abnormality unless the person takes anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Not a primary means of diagnosing important traumatic brain injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Do not use for this purpose before discussion with a neuroscience unit.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The committee considered discharge after shared decision making possible for people under 16 with normal neurological status and no safeguarding concerns. It also considered discharge possible for people 16 and over without safety concerns, except those taking anticoagulants or antiplatelets.

conditions.name: complex skull fracture
conditions.description: The guideline uses this term when describing suspected serious skull injury, including signs associated with basal, open or depressed fracture or penetrating injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Concerning signs include clear fluid from an ear or the nose, an unexplained black eye without surrounding eye injury, bleeding from 1 or both ears, bruising behind 1 or both ears, signs of penetration, or concerning visible scalp or skull trauma.

subtypes.name: basal skull fracture
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Possible signs include haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from an ear or the nose, and Battle's sign.

subtypes.name: open or depressed skull fracture
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Suspicion of either fracture is an urgent head CT criterion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture and associated brain injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Perform within 1 hour of identifying these risk factors under the age-specific head CT criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible non-accidental injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be needed for people under 16 presenting with suspected non-accidental injury.

diagnostic_workup.test: CT or MRI angiography of the neck vessels
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible vascular injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use if vascular injury is suspected because of a high-grade or complex facial fracture or a base of skull fracture likely to involve the internal carotid artery or vertebral artery.

conditions.name: Post-concussion syndrome
conditions.description: A collection of symptoms that can occur after head injuries of any severity and may be under-recognised following mild injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible sensory and motor problems include headache, dizziness, nausea, visual disturbances, altered visual processing, sleepiness, fatigue, sensitivity to noise or light, impaired balance or mobility, and speech problems. Cognitive problems may affect memory, concentration, processing, executive functions, spatial awareness or proprioception. Emotional symptoms may include lability, depression and anxiety. Children under 5 may also show altered behaviour, feeding or sleep, reduced interest in people or objects, or listlessness.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated for predicting post-concussion syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The committee considered the evidence too limited to recommend their predictive use.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated for predicting post-concussion syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The committee considered the evidence too limited to recommend this predictive use.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate clinically important traumatic brain injury when standard head injury criteria indicate imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Apply the age-specific head CT criteria rather than using post-concussion symptoms as a separate imaging rule.

long_term_effects: Persistent sensory, motor, cognitive or emotional difficulties
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Give information about persistent or delayed symptoms and how to seek help. Consider referral to a clinician trained in managing consequences of traumatic brain injury if problems persist.

conditions.name: Hypopituitarism
conditions.description: Reduced pituitary activity that can follow a head injury of any severity. It may become apparent immediately or hours, weeks or months later.
conditions.epidemiology: The committee noted that risk is higher after more severe head injuries, although mild injury can also cause the condition.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations vary by hormone deficiency. Adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency may cause weakness, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia or anaemia. Growth hormone deficiency may cause low energy or mood, cognitive or neuropsychiatric symptoms, altered body composition or metabolism, and reduced exercise capacity. Sex hormone deficiency may cause delayed puberty, hot flushes, loss of body hair, reduced libido, menstrual irregularity, erectile dysfunction or reduced fertility. Thyroid-stimulating hormone deficiency may cause slow growth, fatigue, lethargy, cold intolerance or weight gain. Vasopressin deficiency may cause polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia or incontinence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a biochemical finding that may prompt investigation for hypopituitarism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider investigations in a person admitted after head injury if sodium remains abnormally low.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Persistently low levels are a reason to consider further investigation; they do not establish the diagnosis by themselves.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a clinical finding that may prompt investigation for hypopituitarism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider investigations in a person admitted after head injury if blood pressure remains low.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Persistent hypotension can prompt further investigation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspected pituitary dysfunction after head injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for persistent compatible symptoms presenting in primary or community care in the weeks or months after injury, or for persistently low sodium levels or blood pressure during admission.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess possible hypopituitarism after discharge.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider if compatible symptoms persist or recovery is not as expected.

follow_up.schedule: Symptoms may first appear immediately, hours, weeks or months after the head injury.
recommended_tests: Consider investigations for hypopituitarism for persistent compatible symptoms or persistently low sodium levels or blood pressure.
Consider further endocrinology investigations after discharge if symptoms persist or recovery is not as expected.
long_term_effects: Hormonal, growth, cognitive, metabolic and reproductive difficulties associated with pituitary hormone deficiencies
follow_up.survivorship_notes: In people under 16, the committee emphasised urgent referral to a paediatric endocrinologist when hypopituitarism is suspected.

artifacts.title: Remote advice: referral after head injury
artifacts.source_heading: 1.2 Pre-hospital assessment, advice and referral to hospital — Remote advice services
artifacts.description: Step 1: After a head injury, arrange emergency ambulance transport to an emergency department if the person has impaired consciousness, a focal neurological deficit since the injury, suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating injury, a seizure since the injury, a high-energy head injury, or no other safe means of reaching the emergency department. Step 2: Refer to an emergency department if there has been loss of consciousness followed by recovery, amnesia, persistent headache, vomiting, previous brain surgery, a history of bleeding or clotting disorders, current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment except aspirin monotherapy, drug or alcohol intoxication, a safeguarding concern, irritability or altered behaviour, or continuing diagnostic concern from helpline staff. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5.
artifacts.summary: Distinguishes risk factors requiring an emergency ambulance from those requiring emergency-department referral through a remote advice service.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps remote advisers select the appropriate urgency and means of referral.

artifacts.title: Community assessment and referral after head injury
artifacts.source_heading: 1.2 Pre-hospital assessment, advice and referral to hospital — Community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department
artifacts.description: Step 1: Refer to an emergency department, using an ambulance if necessary, for an initial GCS score of less than 15; loss of consciousness; focal neurological deficit; suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating injury; amnesia; persistent headache; vomiting; seizure; previous brain surgery; high-energy head injury; a history of bleeding or clotting disorders; current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment except aspirin monotherapy; drug or alcohol intoxication; a safeguarding concern; or continuing professional concern about the diagnosis. Use clinical judgement about the cause of vomiting and need for referral in children 12 years or under. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5. Step 2: If none of those factors is present, consider emergency-department referral according to severity when there is irritability or altered behaviour, concerning visible head trauma, nobody able to observe the person at home, or continuing concern from the injured person or their family or carer.
artifacts.summary: Sets out mandatory referral factors and additional circumstances in which community professionals should consider referral.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports decisions in services without an emergency department while preserving clinical judgement for the additional factors.

artifacts.title: Early tranexamic acid decision
artifacts.source_heading: 1.3 Immediate management at the scene and transport to hospital — Tranexamic acid
artifacts.description: Step 1: For a person with head injury and a GCS score of 12 or less who is not thought to have active extracranial bleeding, consider an intravenous bolus of tranexamic acid before imaging and as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury, either before or after arrival at hospital. Step 2: Consider 2 g for people 16 and over; for people under 16, consider 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 2 g. Step 3: If extracranial bleeding is suspected or confirmed, follow the haemostatic-agent recommendations in NICE's guideline on major trauma: assessment and initial management instead. In March 2023, the stated uses of tranexamic acid were off-label.
artifacts.summary: Specifies when tranexamic acid may be considered, with age-dependent bolus doses, timing and the separate route for extracranial bleeding.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Preserves the distinction between considering treatment for head injury without suspected active extracranial bleeding and managing suspected extracranial haemorrhage.

artifacts.title: CT head scan criteria for people 16 and over
artifacts.source_heading: 1.5 Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries — Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People 16 and over
artifacts.description: Step 1: In a person 16 and over with a head injury, perform a CT head scan within 1 hour of identifying any of the following: an initial emergency-department GCS score of 12 or less; a GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; evidence of basal skull fracture, including haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leaking from the ear or nose, or Battle's sign; post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; or more than 1 vomiting episode. Step 2: If the person has had loss of consciousness or amnesia since the injury, perform a CT head scan within 8 hours of injury when any of these factors applies: age 65 or over; a current bleeding or clotting disorder; a pedestrian or cyclist struck by a motor vehicle, ejection from a motor vehicle, or a fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs; or retrograde amnesia for more than 30 minutes immediately before the injury. For someone presenting more than 8 hours after injury with a Step 2 factor, perform the scan within the hour.
artifacts.summary: Separates immediate adult head CT indications from the additional criteria conditional on loss of consciousness or amnesia.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Determines whether head CT is required and which scan deadline applies.

artifacts.title: CT head scan and observation criteria for people under 16
artifacts.source_heading: 1.5 Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries — Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People under 16
artifacts.description: Step 1: For a person under 16 with a head injury, perform CT head imaging within 1 hour of identifying any of these factors: suspected non-accidental injury; post-traumatic seizure; an initial emergency-department GCS score of less than 14, or a paediatric GCS score of less than 15 in a baby under 1 year; a GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture or tense fontanelle; signs of basal skull fracture, including haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leaking from the ear or nose, or Battle's sign; focal neurological deficit; or, in a baby under 1 year, a head bruise, swelling or laceration of more than 5 cm. Step 2: If more than 1 of the following factors is present, perform CT head imaging within 1 hour of identifying them: witnessed loss of consciousness lasting more than 5 minutes; abnormal drowsiness; 3 or more separate vomiting episodes; a high-speed road traffic accident involving a pedestrian, cyclist or vehicle occupant, a fall of more than 3 m, or a high-speed projectile or object injury; anterograde or retrograde amnesia lasting more than 5 minutes; or a current bleeding or clotting disorder. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5. Step 3: If exactly 1 Step 2 factor is present, observe for a minimum of 4 hours from injury. During observation, perform CT head imaging within 1 hour if the GCS score falls below 15, vomiting recurs, or another episode of abnormal drowsiness occurs. Otherwise, use clinical judgement to decide whether observation should continue longer.
artifacts.summary: Provides the paediatric immediate-scan criteria and the separate pathway for multiple versus single additional risk factors.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps avoid both delayed imaging in higher-risk children and automatic imaging when the guideline specifies observation.

artifacts.title: Head CT consideration with anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment
artifacts.source_heading: 1.5 Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries — People taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication
artifacts.description: Step 1: In a person with head injury who has no other indication for head CT, establish whether they are receiving anticoagulant treatment, including vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin or low molecular weight heparins, or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy. Step 2: If so, consider a CT head scan within 8 hours of injury, including when risk assessment is difficult or the person may not return after deterioration. If presentation is more than 8 hours after injury, consider scanning within the hour.
artifacts.summary: Describes when to consider CT solely on the basis of the specified antithrombotic treatments.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Maintains the guideline's 'consider' threshold and its exclusion of aspirin monotherapy from this criterion.

artifacts.title: Cervical spine imaging for people 16 and over
artifacts.source_heading: 1.6 Investigating injuries to the cervical spine — Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people 16 and over
artifacts.description: Step 1: In a person 16 and over with head injury, including delayed presentation, perform cervical spine CT within 1 hour of identifying an initial GCS score of 12 or less, intubation, an urgent need to establish a definitive cervical spine diagnosis, or blunt polytrauma affecting the head and chest, abdomen or pelvis in an alert, stable person. The same deadline applies when cervical spine injury is suspected and the person is age 65 or over, has a dangerous mechanism, a focal peripheral neurological deficit, or paraesthesia in the upper or lower limbs. Dangerous mechanisms are a fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs, an axial head load such as diving, a high-speed motor vehicle collision, rollover, vehicle ejection, an accident involving motorised recreational vehicles, or a bicycle collision. Step 2: For neck pain or tenderness without a Step 1 indication, perform cervical spine CT within 1 hour if neck movement cannot safely be assessed, safe assessment shows inability to actively rotate 45 degrees both left and right, or a condition such as axial spondyloarthritis increases cervical spine injury risk. Step 3: Before imaging, assess neck movement in a person with suspected cervical spine injury only when high-risk factors are absent and at least 1 low-risk feature applies: a simple rear-end vehicle collision, comfort while sitting, walking at any time since injury, no midline cervical tenderness, or delayed neck pain.
artifacts.summary: Organises adult cervical spine CT indications and the restricted circumstances for assessing neck movement before imaging.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Guides imaging urgency without treating neck movement assessment as safe in patients with high-risk factors.

artifacts.title: Cervical spine imaging for people under 16
artifacts.source_heading: 1.6 Investigating injuries to the cervical spine — Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people under 16
artifacts.description: Step 1: In a person under 16 with head injury, including delayed presentation, perform cervical spine CT only if an initial GCS score of 12 or less, intubation, focal peripheral neurological signs, limb paraesthesia, an urgent need for definitive diagnosis, another scan for head injury or multisystem trauma together with suspected cervical spine injury, strong suspicion despite normal X-rays, technically difficult or inadequate X-rays, or significant bony injury on X-rays applies. Perform CT within 1 hour of identifying the factor. Step 2: If there is neck pain or tenderness but no CT indication, obtain 3-view cervical spine X-rays before testing neck movement when there was a dangerous mechanism, safe movement assessment is impossible, or a condition such as collagen vascular disease, osteogenesis imperfecta or axial spondyloarthritis predisposes to cervical spine injury. Dangerous mechanisms are a fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs, an axial head load such as diving, a high-speed motor vehicle collision, rollover, vehicle ejection, an accident involving motorised recreational vehicles, or a bicycle collision. Step 3: If neck movement can safely be assessed in a person with pain or tenderness and no CT indication, obtain 3-view X-rays if they cannot actively rotate 45 degrees both left and right. A peg view may be omitted if the person cannot understand commands or open their mouth. Obtain the indicated X-rays within 1 hour of identifying the factor and have a clinician trained in interpretation review them.
artifacts.summary: Distinguishes the restricted paediatric CT indications from the circumstances requiring cervical spine X-rays.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports age-specific imaging choices and the required time limits.

artifacts.title: Neurosurgical discussion after head injury
artifacts.source_heading: 1.4 Assessment in the emergency department — Involving the neurosurgical department
artifacts.description: Step 1: Discuss care with a neurosurgeon if imaging shows a new surgically significant abnormality, using the locally agreed definition and referral procedure. Step 2: Regardless of imaging results, discuss the care plan if there is persisting coma with a GCS score of 8 or less after initial resuscitation, unexplained confusion persisting more than 4 hours, a decline in GCS score after admission, progressive focal neurological signs, a seizure without full recovery, definite or suspected penetrating injury, or a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Give particular attention to worsening motor response when the GCS score deteriorates.
artifacts.summary: Identifies imaging findings and clinical changes that trigger neurosurgical discussion.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Prevents a normal or unavailable scan from obscuring clinical reasons for specialist consultation.

artifacts.title: Airway and physiological management during transfer to a neuroscience unit
artifacts.source_heading: 1.8 Transfer from hospital to a neuroscience unit — Transfer of people 16 and over
artifacts.description: Step 1: Complete initial resuscitation, stabilise the person and establish comprehensive monitoring before transfer. Do not transport someone with persistent hypotension despite resuscitation until its cause has been identified and the person is stable. Step 2: Intubate and ventilate a person with a GCS score of 8 or less who needs transfer, or immediately if there is coma, loss of protective laryngeal reflexes, ventilatory insufficiency with PaO2 less than 13 kPa on oxygen or PaCO2 more than 6 kPa, or irregular breathing. Step 3: Intubate and ventilate before departure for significantly worsening consciousness, defined here as 1 or more points on the motor score, unstable facial skeletal fractures, substantial bleeding into the mouth, or seizures. Step 4: For an intubated person, provide appropriate sedation, analgesia and a neuromuscular blocking drug. Aim for PaO2 more than 13 kPa and PaCO2 of 4.5 kPa to 5.0 kPa; more aggressive hyperventilation is justified when clinical or radiological evidence indicates raised intracranial pressure, and inspired oxygen concentration should be increased if hyperventilation is used. Maintain mean arterial pressure at 80 mmHg or more using fluids and vasopressors as indicated. Step 5: Apply the stated transfer principles to people under 16, using paediatric GCS modifications for preverbal and non-verbal children, age-appropriate oxygen saturation targets and blood pressure appropriate for age.
artifacts.summary: Sets out stabilisation, intubation and ventilation triggers, physiological targets, and the paediatric modifications for transfer.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports preparation for transfer and identifies conditions requiring airway intervention before or during that process.

artifacts.title: Hospital admission after head injury
artifacts.description: Step 1: Admit after head injury for a new clinically important imaging abnormality; a GCS score that has not returned to 15 or the pre-injury baseline after imaging; an indicated CT scan that cannot be completed within the required time; continuing concerning symptoms such as persistent vomiting, severe headache or seizures; or another clinical concern such as intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism, cerebrospinal fluid leakage or suspected ongoing post-traumatic amnesia. An isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture is unlikely to be clinically important unless the person is taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication. Step 2: For concussion symptoms with normal brain imaging or no indication for early imaging, use those same admission criteria. Step 3: Admit a person with multiple injuries under the team trained to manage the most severe and urgent problem.
artifacts.summary: Collects the admission criteria, including their application to people with concussion symptoms.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps distinguish an imaging result or symptom requiring admission from circumstances in which discharge may be considered.

artifacts.title: Neurological observation and response to deterioration
artifacts.source_heading: 1.9 Admission and observation — Observation of people who are admitted
artifacts.description: Step 1: Document at least the GCS score, pupil size and reactivity, limb movements, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and blood oxygen saturation. Step 2: Observe and record half-hourly until the GCS score reaches 15. For a GCS score of 15, start after the initial emergency-department assessment: observe half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly. If deterioration occurs after the initial 2-hour period, restart half-hourly observations and follow the original schedule. Step 3: Arrange urgent reassessment by a supervising doctor for agitation or abnormal behaviour; a sustained drop of 1 GCS point for at least 30 minutes, with greater weight given to motor-score decline; a drop of 3 or more points in eye-opening or verbal response, or 2 or more points in motor response; severe or worsening headache or persistent vomiting; or new or evolving neurological signs, including unequal pupils or asymmetric facial or limb movement. If immediately possible, first obtain confirmation from another staff member competent in observation; otherwise contact the supervising doctor without waiting. Step 4: If deterioration is confirmed, consider immediate CT, reassess clinically and manage appropriately. If CT was normal but the GCS score remains below 15 after 24 hours of observation, consider further CT or MRI and discuss this with radiology.
artifacts.summary: Provides the minimum observation set, recording frequency and escalation process for neurological deterioration.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Enables timely recognition and reassessment of worsening neurological status during admission.

artifacts.title: Discharge and transfer to community care
artifacts.description: Step 1: When CT is not indicated and clinically important traumatic brain injury is not suspected, discharge if no other admission factor is present and suitable support and subsequent care are available. Step 2: After normal head imaging, transfer to the community if the risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury is low, the GCS score has returned to 15 or its pre-injury baseline, no other admission factor is present, and appropriate support is available. Step 3: After normal cervical spine imaging, transfer to the community if the GCS score is 15, clinical examination is normal, no other admission factor is present, and suitable support is available. Step 4: Do not discharge a person with head injury until the GCS score is 15; for preverbal or non-verbal children, consciousness must be normal according to paediatric GCS, and for people with pre-injury cognitive impairment the score must return to the documented pre-injury level. Step 5: Transfer home only if a suitable person can supervise there; without a carer, discharge only after arranging suitable supervision or when late-complication risk is considered negligible. Following admission, discharge may take place once significant symptoms and signs have resolved and suitable supervision is available at home, in custody or in continued care.
artifacts.summary: Combines the distinct criteria for discharge without CT, after normal head or cervical spine imaging, and after observation.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Makes recovery of consciousness and safe supervision explicit prerequisites where the guideline requires them.

artifacts.title: Printed head injury discharge advice
artifacts.source_heading: 1.10 Discharge and follow up — Discharge advice
artifacts.description: Provide age-appropriate printed advice covering the injury's nature and severity; factors requiring return to the emergency department; the need for a responsible adult to remain with the person during the first 24 hours after injury; recovery, including the possibility of later difficulties despite apparently rapid improvement; contacts for community and hospital services if complications develop later; return to school, work, sports, driving and other usual activities; and support organisations. Give verbal and printed advice to the discharged person and to whoever will be responsible for their care.
artifacts.summary: Lists the required subjects for discharge information and identifies who should receive it.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports recognition of delayed complications and safe care after leaving the emergency department or observation ward.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People seeking remote advice after a head injury.
decision_rules: Arrange emergency ambulance transport to an emergency department if consciousness is absent or incomplete, a focal neurological deficit has occurred since injury, a complex skull fracture or penetrating injury is suspected, a seizure has occurred, the injury involved high energy, or safe transport by other means is unavailable.

Refer to an emergency department if the person has recovered from injury-related loss of consciousness; has amnesia, persistent headache, vomiting, previous brain surgery, a history of bleeding or clotting disorders, current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy, or drug or alcohol intoxication; or if safeguarding concerns, altered behaviour, or continuing diagnostic concern arise.
Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5.

recommended_regimens.name: Emergency ambulance transport
recommended_regimens.summary: Remote advice services should arrange emergency transport to an emergency department when an emergency risk factor is present.

recommended_regimens.name: Referral to a hospital emergency department
recommended_regimens.summary: Remote advice services should direct people with any of the specified additional risk factors to an emergency department.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People assessed by community health services or inpatient units without an emergency department.
decision_rules: Refer to an emergency department if initial GCS is less than 15; injury-related loss of consciousness, focal neurological deficit, suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating injury, amnesia, persistent headache, vomiting, seizure, previous brain surgery, high-energy injury, a history of bleeding or clotting disorders, current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy, intoxication, safeguarding concern, or continuing professional concern is present.

For vomiting in children 12 years or under, use clinical judgement about its cause and whether referral is necessary. Amnesia assessment is not possible in preverbal children and is unlikely to be possible in children under 5.

If none of those risk factors applies, consider emergency department referral according to severity when there is irritability or altered behaviour, concerning visible head trauma, no available observer at home, or continuing concern from the injured person or their family or carer.
Determine whether an ambulance is needed from the person's clinical condition. When it is unnecessary, travel by car or public transport is appropriate if the person is accompanied.

recommended_regimens.name: Referral to a hospital emergency department
recommended_regimens.summary: Community services and inpatient units without emergency facilities should refer people meeting the specified risk criteria, using an ambulance when necessary.

alternative_regimens.name: Referral to a hospital emergency department
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider referral when the specified lower-risk concerns exist without the mandatory-referral risk factors.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The decision depends on clinical judgement of severity.

supportive_care: Ensure that a competent adult accompanies a person referred from community services.
Notify the receiving hospital by phone; for non-emergency transfers, send a written account of signs and symptoms with the person.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People at the scene of injury and during initial transport.
decision_rules: Address the most immediate threat to life first and prevent additional harm.
For people 16 and over, follow the initial trauma-assessment and care principles identified in the guideline; for people under 16, follow the identified paediatric life-support principles.

Use the separate eye-opening, verbal and motor GCS responses for monitoring and communication, alongside a total expressed out of 15. Include the grimace alternative in the paediatric GCS for preverbal children and account for a known pre-injury GCS below 15.
Pre-alert the destination emergency department when GCS is 8 or less.
Transport directly to a major trauma centre or trauma unit with resources appropriate to the person's age for resuscitation, investigation and initial management of multiple injuries.

recommended_regimens.name: Initial assessment and care
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide age-appropriate trauma assessment and immediate care, prioritising life-threatening problems.

recommended_regimens.name: Transport to hospital
recommended_regimens.summary: Take the injured person directly to an appropriately equipped major trauma centre or trauma unit.

response_assessment.timepoint: Initial assessment and throughout communication
response_assessment.method: GCS eye-opening, verbal and motor responses, with total score out of 15
response_assessment.interpretation: Establish the pre-injury baseline when possible and consider it in assessment.

supportive_care: Treat pain effectively because it can increase intracranial pressure; provide reassurance, immobilise limb fractures with splints and catheterise a full bladder when needed.
Follow best practice for observation and recording of paediatric coma.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Refer to the separate NICE major trauma and spinal injury guidelines for volume resuscitation in traumatic brain injury with haemorrhagic shock and for indications and duration of full in-line spine immobilisation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People 16 and over with GCS 12 or less who are not thought to have active extracranial bleeding.
decision_rules: Consider tranexamic acid before imaging, as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury, either before hospital arrival or in hospital.

recommended_regimens.name: tranexamic acid
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider a 2 g intravenous bolus injection before imaging for the specified group. This was an off-label use in March 2023.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited pre-hospital trial, a single 2 g bolus within 2 hours suggested lower all-cause mortality at 28 days and 6 months in moderate or severe traumatic brain injury; the trial found no clinically important difference from placebo in hospital-free days at 28 days, disability at discharge or after 6 months, or serious adverse events.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Single bolus as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For suspected or confirmed extracranial bleeding, the guideline instead directs clinicians to the haemostatic-agent recommendations in NICE's major trauma guideline. The cited evidence leaves the benefit in mild traumatic brain injury uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16 with GCS 12 or less who are not thought to have active extracranial bleeding.
decision_rules: Consider tranexamic acid before imaging, as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury, in a pre-hospital or hospital setting.

recommended_regimens.name: tranexamic acid
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider a 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg intravenous bolus injection, up to a maximum of 2 g. This was an off-label use in March 2023.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Single bolus as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The committee found no trial evidence specifically for people under 16 and extrapolated from adult evidence and clinical experience. For suspected or confirmed extracranial bleeding, follow the haemostatic-agent recommendations in NICE's major trauma guideline.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People presenting to an emergency department after a head injury.
decision_rules: Stabilise airway, breathing and circulation before dealing with other injuries. Do not attribute reduced consciousness to intoxication until important traumatic brain injury has been excluded.
Arrange immediate assessment by trained staff if GCS is less than 15; involve a clinician skilled in advanced airway management early if GCS is 8 or less.
Ensure trained assessment within a maximum of 15 minutes after hospital arrival, including initial risk assessment for clinically important brain and cervical spine injury.
Perform a full examination when risk is high. Re-examine those initially assessed as low risk. Make imaging decisions using the guideline's age-specific criteria after discussion with radiology.
If the person returns with an ongoing complaint related to the injury, reassess, discuss with a senior clinician experienced in head injuries and consider CT.
Consider abuse, neglect and other safeguarding concerns; involve a safeguarding-trained clinician in the initial assessment, document concerns and use age-appropriate local procedures.

recommended_regimens.name: Emergency department assessment
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide prompt, trained clinical assessment and determine subsequent imaging and management from the applicable risk criteria.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within a maximum of 15 minutes of hospital arrival; immediately when GCS is less than 15

response_assessment.timepoint: Initial assessment and subsequent clinical examination
response_assessment.method: GCS and assessment of age-specific CT head and cervical spine risk factors
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the applicable criteria to distinguish people requiring imaging from those who do not.

supportive_care: Treat pain to help avoid increased intracranial pressure; reassure the person, splint limb fractures and catheterise a full bladder when needed.
Use a consistent head-injury documentation form across departments and hospitals, with a separate form for people under 16 and space for additional safeguarding information.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Discuss newly identified, surgically significant imaging abnormalities with a neurosurgeon. Discuss the care plan regardless of imaging if coma with GCS 8 or less persists after resuscitation, unexplained confusion continues for more than 4 hours, GCS deteriorates after admission, focal signs progress, a seizure occurs without full recovery, penetrating injury is definite or suspected, or cerebrospinal fluid leaks.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People 16 and over with any specified high-risk feature after head injury.
decision_rules: Perform CT head imaging if initial emergency department GCS is 12 or less, GCS remains below 15 at 2 hours after injury, an open or depressed skull fracture is suspected, a basal skull fracture sign is present, a post-traumatic seizure or focal neurological deficit occurs, or vomiting occurs more than 1 time.
Signs of basal skull fracture include haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the ear or nose, and Battle's sign.

recommended_regimens.name: CT head scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Image the head when any listed high-risk feature is identified.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

not_recommended.name: MRI scanning
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against using it as the primary investigation for clinically important traumatic brain injury for safety, logistical and resource reasons; it can sometimes provide additional prognostic information.

not_recommended.name: Plain X-rays of the skull
not_recommended.reason: Do not use them to diagnose important traumatic brain injury before discussion with a neuroscience unit.

not_recommended.name: Neuroimaging by direct access from the community
not_recommended.reason: The guideline directs against community direct-access referral after head injury.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 hour of the CT scan
response_assessment.method: Provisional written radiology report

supportive_care: Minimise radiation exposure while retaining the image coverage and quality needed for diagnosis.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Arrange transfer to an appropriate hospital if CT is indicated but unavailable locally.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People 16 and over who have experienced loss of consciousness or amnesia after injury and have an additional specified risk factor.
decision_rules: Perform CT head imaging if the person is aged 65 or over, has a current bleeding or clotting disorder, sustained a dangerous injury mechanism, or has retrograde amnesia for events immediately preceding injury lasting more than 30 minutes.
For this decision, dangerous mechanisms are a motor vehicle striking a pedestrian or cyclist, ejection of an occupant from a motor vehicle, or a fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs.

recommended_regimens.name: CT head scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Image the head when loss of consciousness or amnesia is accompanied by any listed additional risk factor.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour if presentation is more than 8 hours after injury

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 hour of the CT scan
response_assessment.method: Provisional written radiology report

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16 with any specified high-risk feature after head injury.
decision_rules: Perform CT head imaging for suspected non-accidental injury; post-traumatic seizure; initial emergency department GCS below 14, or paediatric GCS below 15 in babies under 1 year; GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture or tense fontanelle; a sign of basal skull fracture; or focal neurological deficit.
In babies under 1 year, also image for a head bruise, swelling or laceration of more than 5 cm.

recommended_regimens.name: CT head scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Image the head when any listed age-specific high-risk feature is present.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

not_recommended.name: MRI scanning
not_recommended.reason: Do not use it as the primary investigation for clinically important traumatic brain injury for safety, logistical and resource reasons.

not_recommended.name: Plain X-rays of the skull
not_recommended.reason: Do not use them to diagnose important traumatic brain injury before discussion with a neuroscience unit; suspected non-accidental injury may instead require a skeletal survey.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 hour of the CT scan
response_assessment.method: Provisional written radiology report

supportive_care: Keep radiation dose as low as practicable without compromising diagnostic image quality and coverage.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Arrange transfer if CT is indicated but not available at the presenting hospital.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16 with more than 1 of the specified additional risk factors.
decision_rules: Image if more than 1 of these is present: witnessed loss of consciousness lasting more than 5 minutes; abnormal drowsiness; 3 or more separate vomiting episodes; dangerous injury mechanism; anterograde or retrograde amnesia lasting more than 5 minutes; or a current bleeding or clotting disorder.
Dangerous mechanisms comprise a high-speed road traffic accident involving a pedestrian, cyclist or vehicle occupant, a fall of more than 3 m, or high-speed impact from a projectile or other object.
Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5.

recommended_regimens.name: CT head scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform head imaging when more than 1 specified risk factor is identified.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factors

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 hour of the CT scan
response_assessment.method: Provisional written radiology report

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16 with only 1 of the risk factors specified for the multiple-risk-factor CT pathway.
decision_rules: Observe initially rather than automatically performing CT.
During observation, perform CT if GCS falls below 15, vomiting recurs or another episode of abnormal drowsiness occurs.
If none occurs, use clinical judgement to decide whether observation should continue longer.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Observe a person with only 1 of the specified risk factors from the time of injury.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Minimum of 4 hours from the time of injury

recommended_regimens.name: CT head scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Image if a specified deterioration feature develops while under observation.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the new risk factor

response_assessment.timepoint: During the minimum 4 hours from the time of injury
response_assessment.method: Assessment of GCS, further vomiting and renewed abnormal drowsiness
response_assessment.interpretation: Any specified new feature triggers CT; without one, decide clinically whether longer observation is necessary.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People of any age without another indication for CT head imaging who receive anticoagulant treatment or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy.
decision_rules: Consider CT for people receiving vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin, low molecular weight heparins, or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy.
Difficulty assessing risk, or concern that the person may not return promptly if they deteriorate, are examples supporting imaging.

The committee's discussion indicates that risk assessment and shared decision making may support discharge without CT when there are no other risks; it does not make medication status alone an automatic CT indication.

recommended_regimens.name: CT head scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider imaging in the absence of another CT indication for people taking the specified treatments.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour when presentation occurs more than 8 hours after injury

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: aspirin monotherapy is excluded from this CT consideration. For traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, the guideline refers elsewhere for advice on reversing vitamin K antagonists and DOACs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People 16 and over, including those presenting late, with a specified high-risk factor for cervical spine injury.
decision_rules: Perform CT cervical spine imaging for initial GCS 12 or less, intubation, an urgent need for a definitive cervical spine diagnosis, or blunt polytrauma affecting the head and chest, abdomen or pelvis in an alert, stable person.

Also image when cervical spine injury is clinically suspected together with age 65 or over, a dangerous injury mechanism, focal peripheral neurological deficit, or paraesthesia in the upper or lower limbs.

recommended_regimens.name: CT cervical spine scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Image the cervical spine for any specified high-risk indication.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 hour of the CT scan
response_assessment.method: Provisional written radiology report
response_assessment.interpretation: Reports should use high-resolution source data and multiplanar reformats covering the entire cervical spine.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The committee did not recommend cervical spine X-rays as the initial imaging approach for people 16 and over with head injury.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People 16 and over with neck pain or tenderness but no high-risk indication for cervical spine CT.
decision_rules: Perform cervical spine CT when assessment of neck movement is unsafe, safe assessment shows inability to rotate actively 45 degrees both left and right, or a condition such as axial spondyloarthritis increases susceptibility to cervical spine injury.

Before imaging, assess neck movement only when high-risk factors are absent and at least 1 low-risk feature is present: simple rear-end collision, comfort while sitting, walking at any time since injury, absence of midline cervical tenderness, or delayed neck pain.

recommended_regimens.name: CT cervical spine scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Image the cervical spine if any specified factor is found in a person with neck symptoms and without a high-risk CT indication.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

response_assessment.timepoint: Before imaging, only when safe to assess
response_assessment.method: Active neck rotation to the left and right
response_assessment.interpretation: Inability to rotate 45 degrees to the left and right is an indication for CT in this population.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16, including those presenting late, with a specified indication for cervical spine CT.
decision_rules: Only perform cervical spine CT if initial GCS is 12 or less; the person has been intubated; focal peripheral neurological signs or limb paraesthesia are present; or a definitive diagnosis is urgently required.

Other indications are concurrent imaging of other body areas for head injury or multisystem trauma with suspected cervical spine injury, strong clinical suspicion despite normal X-rays, technically difficult or inadequate X-rays, or a significant bony injury on X-rays.

recommended_regimens.name: CT cervical spine scan
recommended_regimens.summary: Restrict CT to the listed indications in people under 16.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 hour of the CT scan
response_assessment.method: Provisional written radiology report

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16 with neck pain or tenderness but no indication for cervical spine CT.
