decision_rules: Perform 3-view cervical spine X-rays before testing neck movement when injury followed a dangerous mechanism, safe movement assessment is impossible, or a condition predisposes to cervical spine injury, such as collagen vascular disease, osteogenesis imperfecta or axial spondyloarthritis.
If neck movement can be assessed safely, perform 3-view cervical spine X-rays when the person cannot actively rotate 45 degrees to the left and right.
Assess neck movement before imaging only in the absence of high-risk factors and with at least 1 specified low-risk feature.

recommended_regimens.name: 3-view cervical spine X-rays
recommended_regimens.summary: Obtain cervical spine radiographs for the specified risk factors or restricted active neck rotation, with review by a clinician trained to interpret them.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 hour of identifying the risk factor

response_assessment.timepoint: Before imaging when safe; otherwise after indicated initial X-rays
response_assessment.method: Assessment of active neck rotation
response_assessment.interpretation: Inability to rotate 45 degrees left and right is an indication for radiographs when CT is not otherwise indicated.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A peg view may be left out when the person cannot understand instructions or open their mouth.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People undergoing investigation for suspected associated cervical spine injury.
decision_rules: Add MRI to CT when neurological signs and symptoms suggest cervical spine injury.

Perform CT or MRI angiography of neck vessels if vascular injury is suspected, including with vertebral malalignment, a high-risk facial or skull-base fracture likely to involve the internal carotid or vertebral artery, or posterior circulation syndrome.
Consider MRI when CT or clinical findings suggest ligament or disc injury.

recommended_regimens.name: MRI
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform MRI in addition to CT for neurological features suggesting cervical spine injury.

recommended_regimens.name: CT or MRI angiography
recommended_regimens.summary: Image the neck vessels when vascular injury is suspected.

alternative_regimens.name: MRI
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider additional imaging to assess suspected ligamentous or disc injury.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: CT or clinical findings suggest injury to these structures.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People 16 and over needing transfer from a hospital to a neuroscience unit.
decision_rules: Local transfer arrangements should recognise potential benefit from transfer for serious head injury with GCS 8 or less, regardless of whether neurosurgery is needed. If transfer without a neurosurgical indication is impossible, maintain clinical liaison with the neuroscience unit.
Consider occult injuries outside the head in people with multiple injuries and do not transfer them to a service unable to manage those injuries.

Complete initial resuscitation and stabilisation and establish comprehensive monitoring before departure. Do not transport a person with persistent hypotension despite resuscitation until its cause is identified and the person is stable.

Intubate and ventilate a person needing neuroscience transfer with GCS 8 or less. Intubate and ventilate immediately for coma, lost protective laryngeal reflexes, ventilatory insufficiency with PaO2 less than 13 kPa on oxygen or PaCO2 more than 6 kPa, or irregular breathing.

Intubate and ventilate before travel if consciousness is deteriorating by 1 or more points on the motor score, facial skeletal fractures are unstable, bleeding into the mouth is copious, or seizures occur.

recommended_regimens.name: Transfer to a neuroscience unit
recommended_regimens.summary: Arrange appropriately staffed and monitored transfer under locally agreed procedures after stabilisation.

recommended_regimens.name: Intubation and ventilation
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide airway and ventilatory support for the specified immediate or pre-transfer indications.

not_recommended.name: Transport with persistent hypotension
not_recommended.reason: Do not begin transport despite resuscitation until the cause is established and the person is stabilised, to avoid complications during the journey.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before and during transfer
response_assessment.method: Assessment of haemodynamic stability, neurological status, airway and ventilation
response_assessment.interpretation: Transfer after stabilisation with ongoing monitoring and a means to communicate changes in status.

supportive_care: For an intubated person, provide appropriate sedation, analgesia and a neuromuscular blocking drug.

Aim for PaO2 more than 13 kPa and PaCO2 4.5 kPa to 5.0 kPa; more aggressive hyperventilation is justified when clinical or radiological evidence indicates raised intracranial pressure. If hyperventilating, increase inspired oxygen concentration.
Maintain mean arterial pressure at 80 mmHg or more using fluids and vasopressors as indicated.
Use transfer staff experienced in acute traumatic brain injury, with a trained assistant and a means of communicating with the referring hospital and neurosurgical unit.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Allow family and carers as much access during transfer as practical and, if possible, explain its reasons and process.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People under 16 needing transfer to specialist neurosurgical or tertiary care.
decision_rules: Apply the guideline's principles for transfer, stabilisation, monitoring and indicated intubation and ventilation in people 16 and over to this age group, using the paediatric GCS modification for preverbal and non-verbal children.
Use oxygen-saturation targets and blood-pressure levels appropriate to age rather than the adult transfer targets.
Consider hidden extracranial injuries when injuries are multiple; do not transfer to a service unable to manage other aspects of trauma.
Arrange transfer through staff experienced in transferring critically ill people under 16 or according to local arrangements involving specialist paediatric retrieval teams.

recommended_regimens.name: Transfer to a specialist neurosurgical unit
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide age-appropriate, specialist-staffed transfer following the applicable adult transfer principles and paediatric service standards.

not_recommended.name: Transfer to a service unable to manage other aspects of trauma
not_recommended.reason: Occult extracranial injury may be present in a person with multiple injuries.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before and during transfer
response_assessment.method: Paediatric GCS when applicable, age-appropriate oxygen saturation and blood pressure, and monitoring of clinical stability

supportive_care: Give families and carers as much practical access to the child during transfer as possible and, when feasible, explain why and how transfer will occur.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with indications for admission following head injury, including those with concussion symptoms after normal brain imaging or without an indication for early imaging.
decision_rules: Admit for a new clinically important imaging abnormality; GCS that has not returned to 15 or the pre-injury baseline after imaging; indicated CT that cannot be completed within the required time; continuing concerning symptoms; or another clinical concern such as intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism, cerebrospinal fluid leak or suspected ongoing post-traumatic amnesia.
An isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture is unlikely to constitute a clinically important imaging abnormality unless the person takes anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication.
Use the same admission criteria for people with concussion symptoms when imaging is normal or early imaging is not indicated.
For multiple injuries, place the person under the team equipped to address the most severe and urgent problem.

recommended_regimens.name: Hospital admission
recommended_regimens.summary: Admit when any specified imaging, consciousness, imaging-access, symptom or other clinical concern warrants inpatient care.

response_assessment.timepoint: Following imaging and during admission assessment
response_assessment.method: Imaging findings, GCS relative to 15 or pre-injury baseline, symptoms and other clinical concerns
response_assessment.interpretation: An applicable admission criterion supports hospital care.

supportive_care: Place an admitted person under a consultant-led team trained in assessment, observation, imaging decisions, inpatient management, neuroscience-unit transfer, discharge and follow up.
Allow for an extended recovery period when general anaesthesia was required for CT.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The committee did not consider age, frailty, anticoagulant treatment or antiplatelet treatment alone sufficient as an admission criterion after a negative initial CT; these points are discussed in the rationale rather than set out as separate admission criteria.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People admitted to hospital for observation after head injury.
decision_rules: Document at least GCS, pupil size and response, limb movements, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and blood oxygen saturation.
Observe half-hourly until GCS reaches 15. At GCS 15, use half-hourly observations for 2 hours, then 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly.
If a person with GCS 15 deteriorates after the initial 2-hour period, return to half-hourly monitoring and repeat the original frequency schedule.

Arrange urgent reassessment by a supervising doctor for agitation or abnormal behaviour; a sustained fall of 1 GCS point for at least 30 minutes, especially in motor response; a fall of 3 or more points in eye-opening or verbal response or 2 or more points in motor response; severe or worsening headache or persistent vomiting; or new or evolving neurological signs.
Seek immediate confirmation of deterioration from another competent observer when possible; do not delay contact with the supervising doctor if a second observer is unavailable.

If deterioration is confirmed, consider immediate CT, reassess clinically and manage accordingly. If initial CT was normal but GCS has not reached 15 after 24 hours of observation, consider repeat CT or MRI after discussion with radiology.

recommended_regimens.name: In-hospital observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Use competent staff to conduct and document neurological and physiological observations at the specified frequencies.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Half-hourly until GCS 15; at GCS 15, half-hourly for 2 hours, 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly

alternative_regimens.name: CT or MRI scan
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider further imaging when GCS has not reached 15 despite observation after a normal CT.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: After 24 hours of observation, following discussion with radiology.

response_assessment.timepoint: At each scheduled observation
response_assessment.method: Documented GCS components, pupils, limb movements and vital signs
response_assessment.interpretation: The specified behavioural, GCS, headache, vomiting or focal neurological changes require urgent reassessment.

response_assessment.timepoint: After 24 hours of observation following a normal CT
response_assessment.method: GCS assessment
response_assessment.interpretation: GCS below 15 prompts consideration of further CT or MRI.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Observe babies and children under 5 only in units with staff experienced in observing head injury in this age group; an ordinary paediatric observation setting is acceptable when that expertise is available.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People admitted after head injury with persistently low sodium or low blood pressure; people in primary or community care with persistent compatible symptoms weeks or months later; and discharged people with persistent compatible symptoms or slower-than-expected recovery.
decision_rules: Consider investigation for hypopituitarism in admitted people whose sodium remains abnormally low or whose blood pressure remains low.
In primary or community care, consider investigation or referral when compatible symptoms persist in the weeks or months after head injury.
After discharge, consider further endocrinology investigation for persistent compatible symptoms or recovery that does not proceed as expected.

recommended_regimens.name: Investigations for hypopituitarism
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider assessment for pituitary dysfunction in the specified inpatient or later-care circumstances.

alternative_regimens.name: Referral for hypopituitarism
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider referral instead of investigation in primary or community care for persistent compatible symptoms.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptoms continue in the weeks or months after head injury.

response_assessment.timepoint: During admission or in the weeks or months after injury
response_assessment.method: Clinical assessment for compatible symptoms, sodium and blood pressure when applicable, and evaluation of recovery
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent abnormalities or compatible symptoms support consideration of investigation or referral.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Pituitary dysfunction can follow a head injury of any severity and may become apparent immediately or later. The committee emphasised urgent referral to a paediatric endocrinologist when hypopituitarism is suspected in a person under 16.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People being considered for discharge without CT head imaging, after normal head imaging, or after normal cervical spine imaging.
decision_rules: If CT is not indicated by history and examination and clinically important traumatic brain injury is not suspected, discharge only when no other admission factor exists and suitable support for safe care in the community is available.

After normal head imaging and low risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury, transfer to the community only when GCS has returned to 15 or the pre-injury baseline, no other admission factor is present and suitable support is available.
After normal cervical spine imaging, community transfer is appropriate when GCS is 15, the clinical examination is normal, no other admission factor is present and suitable support is available.

Do not discharge until GCS is 15; for preverbal or non-verbal children, consciousness must be normal on the paediatric GCS; for people with pre-injury cognitive impairment, GCS must return to its documented pre-injury level.
Transfer home only if a suitable person can supervise. Without a carer at home, discharge only if appropriate supervision has been arranged or late-complication risk is considered negligible.

recommended_regimens.name: Discharge to the community
recommended_regimens.summary: Discharge or transfer to community care when the applicable imaging, clinical and supervision conditions are satisfied.

not_recommended.name: Discharge before recovery of consciousness
not_recommended.reason: The guideline requires GCS 15, normal paediatric GCS consciousness when applicable, or return to the documented pre-injury GCS in people with cognitive impairment.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before discharge
response_assessment.method: GCS or paediatric GCS, applicable imaging and clinical examination, admission factors and availability of supervision
response_assessment.interpretation: Discharge requires all conditions relevant to the person's imaging pathway and safe ongoing care to be met.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: People with pre-injury cognitive impairment and people returning to custody need supervision, monitoring and arrangements to respond to deterioration.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People admitted for observation whose significant signs and symptoms have resolved.
decision_rules: Discharge may take place once all significant symptoms and signs have resolved, provided suitable supervision is arranged at home, in custody or in continuing care.

recommended_regimens.name: Discharge after observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider discharge after clinical resolution and confirmation of appropriate supervision.

response_assessment.timepoint: At the end of observation
response_assessment.method: Assessment of significant symptoms and signs and supervision arrangements
response_assessment.interpretation: Resolution of significant findings with suitable supervision permits discharge.

supportive_care: Give verbal and printed, age-appropriate head-injury advice to the person and whoever will be responsible for their care.

Specify in printed advice that a responsible adult should stay for the first 24 hours after injury; include reasons to return to the emergency department, possible delayed difficulties, recovery information, contacts and guidance on everyday activities.

For anyone seen in the emergency department, write to their GP within 48 hours of discharge with clinical history and examination findings; also share the letter with health visitors for preschool children and school nurses for school-age children and young people.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Offer information on alcohol or drug misuse when a person who presented intoxicated is fit for discharge. Explain that symptoms can persist or emerge later and identify whom to contact.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People after head injury who have persistent problems, possible contributing causes of injury, or symptoms suggestive of hypopituitarism after discharge.
decision_rules: Refer when appropriate to investigate why the injury occurred or address contributing factors, including consideration of falls assessment or safeguarding services.

Consider referral for continuing problems to a clinician trained in consequences of traumatic brain injury, such as a neurologist, neuropsychologist, clinical psychologist, neurosurgeon or endocrinologist, or a multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation team.
For persistent symptoms compatible with hypopituitarism or recovery that is not as expected after discharge, consider further endocrinology investigations.

recommended_regimens.name: Follow up
recommended_regimens.summary: Arrange appropriate investigation and referral for causes of injury, contributing factors or persistent consequences.

response_assessment.timepoint: During follow up
response_assessment.method: Assessment of persisting problems, recovery, possible pituitary symptoms and factors contributing to the injury
response_assessment.interpretation: Findings guide consideration of specialist referral or further investigation.

supportive_care: Ensure that people and carers know whom to contact for persistent or delayed symptoms.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Persistent physical, sensory, motor, cognitive, emotional or hormonal problems can occur even when initial imaging was normal or the person was not admitted.

special_populations.considerations: Use the paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) when assessing consciousness. A score of less than 15 on initial emergency department assessment, or a head bruise, swelling or laceration of more than 5 cm, is an indication for a CT head scan within 1 hour. Observation requires staff experienced in assessing young children.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: If head injury is accompanied by a GCS score of 12 or less and active extracranial bleeding is not suspected, consider a 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 2 g) intravenous bolus injection of tranexamic acid as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury, before imaging.

special_populations.considerations: Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children. The paediatric GCS provides a 'grimace' alternative to the verbal response. Before discharge, consciousness should be normal when assessed with the paediatric GCS.

Amnesia is unlikely to be assessable. Irritability, altered behaviour, changes in feeding or sleep, reduced interest and listlessness may be relevant after injury. Observation is difficult and should be undertaken only in units whose staff have experience observing this age group after a head injury.

Assessment, CT head and cervical spine imaging criteria, observation and transfer have age-specific provisions. With only 1 of the risk factors in recommendation 1.5.11, observe for a minimum of 4 hours from injury and obtain a CT head scan within 1 hour if a GCS score of less than 15, further vomiting or another episode of abnormal drowsiness occurs. For cervical spine assessment, 3-view cervical spine X-rays are indicated in specified circumstances when CT criteria are absent. If hypopituitarism is suspected, the committee emphasises urgent referral to a paediatric endocrinologist.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For head injury with a GCS score of 12 or less and no suspected active extracranial bleeding, consider a 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 2 g) intravenous bolus injection of tranexamic acid as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury and before imaging. During transfer, use age-appropriate oxygen saturation and blood pressure targets rather than the targets specified for people 16 and over.

special_populations.considerations: Separate adult criteria govern CT head and cervical spine scans. A CT head scan is indicated within 1 hour for specified high-risk findings; after loss of consciousness or amnesia, other specified factors call for scanning within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour when presentation is more than 8 hours after injury. Transfer and airway-management guidance includes provisions for severe traumatic brain injury.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For head injury with a GCS score of 12 or less and no suspected active extracranial bleeding, consider a 2 g intravenous bolus injection of tranexamic acid as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury and before imaging.

special_populations.population: People taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy
special_populations.considerations: Treatment is a factor in referral after head injury. When there is no other indication for CT head imaging, consider scanning within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour if presentation occurs more than 8 hours after injury. The committee describes risk assessment and shared decision making as relevant to whether a person with otherwise low-risk findings can leave without scanning. Medication status alone was not considered a sufficient reason for admission after a negative initial CT scan.

Aspirin monotherapy is excluded from the medication-specific CT consideration. The committee states that, after shared decision making, discharge without a CT head scan is possible if no other indication for scanning or hospital admission applies.

special_populations.population: People with current bleeding or clotting disorders
special_populations.considerations: A current disorder is a factor in CT head decisions after loss of consciousness or amnesia in people 16 and over, and in the assessment of multiple risk factors for people under 16. The committee reports no evidence specific to people with liver or coagulopathy disorders and notes that acquired coagulation defects form a varied group.

special_populations.population: People with pre-injury cognitive impairment or learning disabilities
special_populations.considerations: Establish a pre-injury GCS baseline when possible because it may be less than 15, and account for it during assessment. Symptoms, loss of consciousness and amnesia may be difficult to recognise or assess. Before discharge, the GCS score should have returned to the documented pre-injury level. Arrange supervision and monitoring after discharge, with a plan for deterioration; the committee describes overnight observation when supervision at home is unavailable.

special_populations.population: People returning to a custodial setting
special_populations.considerations: Ensure supervision and monitoring after discharge, together with arrangements for responding to deterioration. Discharge advice should reach the person responsible for their care.

special_populations.population: People with possible non-accidental injury or other safeguarding concerns
special_populations.considerations: Safeguarding concerns affect referral, imaging assessment and admission decisions. Involve a clinician trained in safeguarding in the initial emergency department assessment, document concerns and follow local procedures appropriate to age. A person under 16 with suspected non-accidental injury meets a CT head criterion and may need a skeletal survey.

Consider injuries outside the skull that may not initially be apparent. Do not transfer a person to a service unable to manage the other aspects of their trauma. For hospital admission, the team responsible should be trained to address the most severe and urgent problem.

After normal brain imaging or when early imaging is not indicated, apply the usual head-injury admission criteria. The committee notes that most people with normal imaging and concussion symptoms do not need further intervention, while discharge advice should address delayed or persistent problems.

special_populations.population: People with suspected hypopituitarism after a head injury
special_populations.considerations: Pituitary dysfunction can follow a head injury of any severity and can appear immediately or later. For admitted people with persistently low sodium levels or low blood pressure, consider investigation. In primary or community care, consider investigation or referral for persistent compatible symptoms in the weeks or months after injury. After discharge, consider further endocrinology investigation if compatible symptoms persist or recovery is not as expected.
The committee identified no evidence specific to recurrent head injuries in any age group and proposed research on imaging indications when no other CT indication is present.

special_populations.population: People presenting more than 24 hours after a head injury
special_populations.considerations: The committee describes limited evidence for delayed presentation and proposed research on selecting people of any age for CT or MRI head imaging. It agreed that the existing CT head recommendations could be extrapolated to presentation more than 24 hours after injury.

special_populations.population: People without suitable supervision at home
special_populations.considerations: Home discharge requires someone suitable to supervise the injured person. If no carer is available, discharge only when suitable supervision has been arranged or the risk of late complications is considered negligible.

recommendations.statement: For guidance on involving healthcare professionals and service users in treatment and care decisions, consult NICE's guideline on shared decision making.
recommendations.rationale: The committee emphasised involving people with a head injury and their families and carers in care decisions.

recommendations.statement: For decisions involving people 16 and over who may lack capacity now or later, including advance care plans, consult NICE's guideline on decision making and mental capacity.
recommendations.rationale: The committee highlighted the importance of decisions for people who may lack capacity and of following advance care plans.

recommendations.statement: Public health materials and non-medical advisers should encourage anyone concerned about their own or another person's head injury to obtain immediate medical advice, regardless of apparent severity.
recommendations.source_heading: Pre-hospital assessment, advice and referral to hospital

recommendations.statement: Remote advice services should arrange emergency ambulance transport to an emergency department after a head injury if the person is unconscious or not fully conscious, has had a focal neurological deficit or seizure since injury, has a suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating head injury, has sustained a high-energy head injury, or cannot otherwise be transported safely to the emergency department.

Remote advice services should refer a person with a head injury to an emergency department if there has been injury-related loss of consciousness followed by recovery; amnesia before or after injury; persistent headache; any vomiting; previous brain surgery; a history of bleeding or clotting disorders; current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy; current drug or alcohol intoxication; safeguarding concerns; irritability or altered behaviour, particularly in babies and children under 5; or continuing diagnostic concern among helpline staff. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5.

Community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department should refer a person with a head injury to a hospital emergency department, using an ambulance if needed, for an initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of less than 15; any injury-related loss of consciousness; focal neurological deficit; suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating head injury; pre- or post-injury amnesia; persistent headache; any vomiting; seizure; previous brain surgery; high-energy head injury; a history of bleeding or clotting disorders; current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment other than aspirin monotherapy; intoxication; safeguarding concerns; or continuing professional concern about the diagnosis. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5. For vomiting in children 12 years or under, use clinical judgement about its cause and whether referral is needed.
recommendations.source_heading: Community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department

recommendations.statement: If none of the factors in recommendation 1.2.4 is present, consider emergency department referral according to severity when there is irritability or altered behaviour, particularly in babies and children under 5; visible head trauma that still concerns the professional; nobody available to observe the person at home; or continuing concern about the diagnosis from the person or their family or carer.
recommendations.source_heading: Community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department

recommendations.statement: Ensure that a competent adult accompanies anyone referred from community health services while they travel to the emergency department.
recommendations.source_heading: Transport to hospital from community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department

recommendations.statement: The referring professional should decide whether the clinical condition requires an ambulance; if not, accompanied travel by public transport or car is appropriate.
recommendations.source_heading: Transport to hospital from community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department

recommendations.statement: The referring professional should telephone the receiving hospital about the transfer and, for a non-emergency transfer, send a letter describing the signs and symptoms with the person.
recommendations.source_heading: Transport to hospital from community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department

recommendations.statement: Train GPs, nurse practitioners, dentists and ambulance crews as needed to assess the risk factors specified for community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department.

Use the 3 individual GCS responses when monitoring and communicating about head injury; for example, a total score of 13 comprising eye opening 4, verbal response 4 and motor response 5 should be reported as E4, V4, M5.
Report a total GCS score as a score out of 15, for example, 13 out of 15.
Include each GCS component alongside the total score in every clinical record and communication.
Use a 'grimace' alternative to the verbal component of the paediatric GCS when scoring preverbal children.
Where possible, establish and account for a pre-injury GCS baseline below 15, which can occur with dementia, chronic neurological disorders or learning disabilities.

Initially assess and manage people 16 and over with a head injury according to established principles represented by the Advanced Trauma Life Support course or European Trauma course, International Trauma Life Support course, Pre-hospital Trauma Life Support course, Advanced Trauma Nurse Course, Trauma Nursing Core Course, or Joint Royal Colleges Ambulance Service Liaison Committee Clinical Practice Guidelines for Head Trauma.

Initially assess and manage people under 16 with a head injury according to the principles of the Advanced Paediatric Life Support course or European Paediatric Life Support course, Pre-hospital Paediatric Life Support course, or Paediatric Education for Pre-hospital Professionals course.

During immediate care, address the greatest threat to life first and prevent additional harm; consult NICE's major trauma guideline for volume resuscitation in traumatic brain injury with haemorrhagic shock.
Consult NICE's spinal injury guideline for indications and duration of full in-line spine immobilisation.
Pre-alert the receiving emergency department when a person's GCS score is 8 or less so that appropriately experienced clinicians and imaging preparations are available.
Treat pain effectively to limit rises in intracranial pressure; provide reassurance, immobilise limb fractures and catheterise a full bladder when needed.
recommendations.rationale: Pain can raise intracranial pressure.

recommendations.statement: Follow the National Paediatric Neuroscience Benchmarking Group's best practice for observing and recording paediatric coma.
Take people with a head injury directly to a major trauma centre or trauma unit equipped for their age to continue resuscitation and investigate and initially manage multiple injuries.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence comparing specialist and non-specialist destinations was limited and uncertain; the committee found no compelling basis for changing established transport practice.

recommendations.statement: Consult NICE's guideline on major trauma: service delivery for care of people with major trauma.
Fully train ambulance crews and paramedics to use and score the adult and paediatric GCS.
recommendations.source_heading: Training for ambulance crews and paramedics

recommendations.statement: Train ambulance crews and paramedics in safeguarding people under 16 and vulnerable people 16 and over; require them to record concerns and communicate them verbally to emergency department staff.
recommendations.source_heading: Training for ambulance crews and paramedics

recommendations.statement: For head injury with a GCS score of 12 or less and no suspected active extracranial bleeding, consider an intravenous bolus of tranexamic acid: 2 g for people 16 and over, or 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 2 g) for people under 16. Administer as soon as possible within 2 hours of injury, before imaging, either before hospital arrival or in hospital. In March 2023, these uses were off-label.
recommendations.rationale: Adult trial evidence suggested reduced mortality in relevant traumatic brain injury groups; the paediatric dose was informed by extrapolation from adults and clinical experience, with no trial evidence for people under 16.

recommendations.statement: For head injury accompanied by suspected or confirmed extracranial bleeding, consult the haemostatic-agent recommendations for pre-hospital and hospital care in NICE's guideline on major trauma: assessment and initial management.
Do not use direct community referral for neuroimaging after a head injury.
recommendations.rationale: The committee identified no comparative evidence and noted difficulties obtaining timely imaging and reports and interpreting complex reports in community care.
recommendations.source_heading: Direct access from the community to imaging

recommendations.statement: For every emergency department attendee, stabilise airway, breathing and circulation before addressing other injuries.
Do not attribute depressed consciousness to intoxication until important traumatic brain injury has been excluded.

Ensure emergency department clinicians assessing head injury can identify the specified risk factors for CT imaging of the head and cervical spine in people 16 and over and under 16; provide training where necessary.
Have trained staff immediately assess emergency department attendees with impaired consciousness, defined as a GCS score of less than 15.
For a GCS score of 12 or less, consult the tranexamic acid recommendations.
For a GCS score of 8 or less, involve an appropriately trained clinician early for advanced airway management and resuscitation support, as described in recommendations 1.8.7 and 1.8.8.

Have trained staff assess every emergency department attendee with a head injury within a maximum of 15 minutes after arrival, including classification of risk for clinically important traumatic brain or cervical spine injury using the relevant age-specific CT criteria.

For people at high risk of clinically important traumatic brain or cervical spine injury, perform a full clinical examination to determine whether imaging of the head, cervical spine or other areas is needed; base the final imaging decision on the relevant age-specific CT criteria after discussion with radiology.

An emergency department clinician should re-examine people initially classified as low risk for clinically important traumatic brain or cervical spine injury and determine the need for head or cervical spine CT using the age-specific criteria after discussion with radiology.

Reassess anyone returning to an emergency department with a persistent complaint related to their original head injury, discuss the case with a senior clinician experienced in head injuries, and consider CT.
Manage pain effectively to help avert increased intracranial pressure; offer reassurance, splint limb fractures and catheterise a full bladder when necessary.
recommendations.rationale: Pain may increase intracranial pressure.

recommendations.statement: Consider whether abuse, neglect or other safeguarding issues contributed to or caused the head injury; consult the relevant NICE safeguarding guidelines for associated clinical features.
recommendations.rationale: The committee emphasised following relevant guidance when maltreatment or other safeguarding concerns may be involved.

recommendations.statement: Include a safeguarding-trained clinician in the initial emergency department assessment of a person with head injury; document any concerns and follow age-appropriate local safeguarding procedures.

Use a consistently formatted standard head injury proforma throughout hospital assessment and observation, with a separate form for people under 16 and space for additional details such as nonaccidental injury.

Discuss the care of anyone with newly identified, surgically significant imaging abnormalities with a neurosurgeon; local neurosurgical centres and referring hospitals should agree on the definition and referral arrangements.

Discuss the care plan with a neurosurgeon regardless of imaging when a person has persistent coma after initial resuscitation (GCS score of 8 or less), unexplained confusion lasting more than 4 hours, a deteriorating GCS score after admission—particularly the motor component—progressive focal neurological signs, a seizure without complete recovery, definite or suspected penetrating injury, or a cerebrospinal fluid leak.
Use head CT as the primary investigation for acute clinically important traumatic brain injury.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: Do not use MRI as the primary investigation for clinically important traumatic brain injury after head injury, for safety, logistical and resource reasons; it may nevertheless reveal additional prognostic information.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline cites safety, logistics and resource use as reasons against primary MRI.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: Provide suitable monitoring equipment during MRI for people with head injury, and ensure all involved staff know the hazards and precautions associated with proximity to the scanner.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: Do not use plain skull X-rays to diagnose important traumatic brain injury without first discussing the case with a neuroscience unit; a skeletal survey may be needed for a person under 16 with suspected non-accidental injury.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: Transfer people who meet CT indications to a suitable hospital if CT is unavailable at the presenting hospital.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: Trauma networks should provide for the transfers required when an indicated CT scan is unavailable at the presenting hospital.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: Minimise radiation exposure when imaging the head and cervical spine while retaining the quality and anatomical coverage needed for diagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries

recommendations.statement: For people 16 and over with head injury, obtain head CT within 1 hour after identifying any of these factors: initial emergency department GCS score of 12 or less; emergency department GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; signs of basal skull fracture, including haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid from the ear or nose, or Battle's sign; post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; or more than 1 vomiting episode.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered the evidence insufficient to change the existing adult head-imaging decision rules.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People 16 and over

recommendations.statement: For people 16 and over who have experienced loss of consciousness or amnesia since a head injury, obtain head CT within 8 hours of injury—or within the hour if presentation is more than 8 hours after injury—if they are age 65 or over, have a current bleeding or clotting disorder, sustained a dangerous mechanism of injury (pedestrian or cyclist hit by a motor vehicle, vehicle occupant ejected, or fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs), or have more than 30 minutes' retrograde amnesia immediately preceding the injury.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered the evidence insufficient to change the existing adult head-imaging decision rules.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People 16 and over

recommendations.statement: For people under 16 with head injury, obtain head CT within 1 hour after identifying suspected non-accidental injury; post-traumatic seizure; initial emergency department GCS score of less than 14, or paediatric GCS score of less than 15 for babies under 1 year; GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture or tense fontanelle; signs of basal skull fracture, including haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid from the ear or nose, or Battle's sign; focal neurological deficit; or, in babies under 1 year, a head bruise, swelling or laceration of more than 5 cm.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered the evidence insufficient to change the existing imaging decision rules for people under 16.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People under 16

recommendations.statement: For a person under 16 with head injury and more than 1 of the following factors, obtain head CT within 1 hour after identifying them: witnessed loss of consciousness lasting more than 5 minutes; abnormal drowsiness; 3 or more separate vomiting episodes; dangerous injury mechanism (high-speed road collision affecting a pedestrian, cyclist or vehicle occupant, fall of more than 3 m, or high-speed impact from a projectile or other object); anterograde or retrograde amnesia lasting more than 5 minutes; or a current bleeding or clotting disorder. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People under 16

recommendations.statement: If a person under 16 with head injury has only 1 factor from recommendation 1.5.11, observe them for a minimum of 4 hours from injury. Obtain head CT within 1 hour if observation identifies a GCS score of less than 15, further vomiting or another episode of abnormal drowsiness. Otherwise, use clinical judgement about longer observation.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People under 16

recommendations.statement: For head injury with no other head CT indication in someone receiving anticoagulants—including vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin and low molecular weight heparins—or antiplatelets other than aspirin monotherapy, consider head CT within 8 hours of injury, including when risk assessment is difficult or return after deterioration is doubtful; if presentation occurs more than 8 hours after injury, consider CT within the hour. Consult the specified NICE and MHRA guidance for reversal advice concerning vitamin K antagonists and DOACs.
recommendations.rationale: The committee judged the evidence insufficient to stop considering imaging in this group but changed the approach from routine scanning to individual consideration.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — People taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication

recommendations.statement: Provide a provisional written radiology report within 1 hour after CT.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan — Timing of radiology report

recommendations.statement: For referral information concerning possible post-concussion syndrome, consult recommendation 1.10.14 on follow up.
recommendations.rationale: The committee found insufficient evidence to recommend biomarkers or MRI for predicting post-concussion syndrome.

recommendations.statement: Before imaging, assess neck movement in a person with head injury and suspected cervical spine injury only when no high-risk factors are present and at least 1 low-risk feature applies: a simple rear-end vehicle collision, comfortable sitting, walking at any time since injury, no midline cervical tenderness, or delayed onset of neck pain.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessing range of movement in the neck

recommendations.statement: For a person 16 and over with head injury, including delayed presentation, obtain cervical spine CT within 1 hour of identifying initial GCS score of 12 or less; intubation; urgent need for a definitive cervical spine diagnosis; blunt polytrauma affecting the head and chest, abdomen or pelvis in an alert, stable person; or suspected cervical spine injury together with age 65 or over, a dangerous injury mechanism, focal peripheral neurological deficit, or upper- or lower-limb paraesthesia. Dangerous mechanisms include a fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs, axial head loading such as diving, high-speed vehicle collision, rollover, vehicle ejection, an accident involving motorised recreational vehicles, or bicycle collision.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered CT preferable to initial cervical spine X-rays for people 16 and over; the available evidence suggested poorer sensitivity with X-rays.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people 16 and over

recommendations.statement: For a person 16 and over with head injury and neck pain or tenderness but no high-risk CT indication, obtain cervical spine CT within 1 hour if neck movement cannot safely be assessed, safe assessment shows inability to actively rotate 45 degrees to both left and right, or a condition such as axial spondyloarthritis increases cervical spine injury risk.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people 16 and over

recommendations.statement: For a person under 16 with head injury, including delayed presentation, perform cervical spine CT only for an initial GCS score of 12 or less; intubation; focal peripheral neurological signs; paraesthesia in upper or lower limbs; urgent need for a definitive cervical spine diagnosis; scanning of other body areas for head injury or multisystem trauma together with suspected cervical spine injury; strong clinical suspicion despite normal X-rays; technically difficult or inadequate X-rays; or significant bony injury on X-rays. Perform CT within 1 hour after the factor is identified.
recommendations.rationale: For people under 16, the committee considered limitations of the evidence alongside radiation exposure and cancer risk.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people under 16

recommendations.statement: For a person under 16 with head injury and neck pain or tenderness but no cervical spine CT indication, obtain 3-view cervical spine X-rays before neck movement assessment if there was a dangerous mechanism, movement cannot safely be assessed, or a condition such as collagen vascular disease, osteogenesis imperfecta or axial spondyloarthritis increases cervical spine injury risk. Dangerous mechanisms include a fall of more than 1 m or 5 stairs, axial head loading such as diving, high-speed vehicle collision, rollover, vehicle ejection, an accident involving motorised recreational vehicles, or bicycle collision. Complete X-rays within 1 hour after identifying the factor and have a clinician trained in interpretation review them.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people under 16

recommendations.statement: For a person under 16 with head injury and neck pain or tenderness but no cervical spine CT indication, if neck movement can safely be assessed and they cannot actively rotate 45 degrees to both left and right, obtain 3-view cervical spine X-rays within 1 hour and have them reviewed by a clinician trained in interpretation. A peg view may be omitted if the person cannot understand commands or open their mouth.
recommendations.source_heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people under 16

recommendations.statement: Make a provisional written radiology report available within 1 hour after CT.
Base cervical spine imaging reports on high-resolution source data and multiplanar reformats covering the entire cervical spine.
Add MRI to CT when neurological signs and symptoms suggest cervical spine injury.

Perform CT or MRI angiography of neck vessels when vascular injury is suspected, for example with vertebral malalignment, a high-risk fracture such as a high-grade or complex facial fracture or skull base fracture likely to involve the internal carotid artery or vertebral artery, or posterior circulation syndrome.
Consider MRI to assess ligament or disc injury suggested by CT or clinical findings.
Staff caring for a person with head injury should introduce themselves to family members and carers and briefly describe their activities.
recommendations.source_heading: Information and support for families and carers

recommendations.statement: Explain the injury's nature and the likely course of care in information given to families and carers.
recommendations.source_heading: Information and support for families and carers

recommendations.statement: Staff should consider how to communicate with people under 16 about the possibility of complex long-term changes in an injured parent or sibling; patient-support-group literature may help.
recommendations.source_heading: Information and support for families and carers

recommendations.statement: Encourage relatives and carers to speak with and touch the injured person, such as by holding hands, without making them feel required to remain at the bedside for extended periods; encourage regular breaks if they choose to stay.
recommendations.source_heading: Information and support for families and carers

recommendations.statement: Provide a display area with leaflets or contact information for local and national patient-support organisations for families and carers.
recommendations.source_heading: Information and support for families and carers

recommendations.statement: Referring hospital trusts, neuroscience units and local ambulance services should jointly establish transfer guidance for severe traumatic brain injury, recognising that transfer would benefit anyone with serious head injury and a GCS score of 8 or less irrespective of neurosurgical need; if transfer without neurosurgical need is impossible, maintain ongoing clinical liaison with the neuroscience unit.
In multiply injured people 16 and over, consider hidden extracranial injuries and do not transfer them to a service unable to manage their other trauma.

Designate a consultant at the referring hospital to arrange transfers to a neuroscience unit and a consultant at that unit to arrange communication with referring hospitals and receive transferred people.

Accompany emergency transfers for traumatic brain injury with healthcare staff experienced and trained in acute traumatic brain injury transfer who understand its pathophysiology, their medicines and equipment, and working in an ambulance or, where appropriate, helicopter; provide a dedicated trained assistant, suitable clothing, medical indemnity and personal accident insurance. Use appropriate clinical staff to accompany non-emergency transfers.
Equip the transfer team to communicate changes in the injured person's condition to its base hospital and the neurosurgical unit during transfer.

Before transfer, finish initial resuscitation and stabilisation and establish comprehensive monitoring, despite urgency. Do not transport someone with persistent hypotension despite resuscitation until its cause is known and the person is stabilised.
recommendations.rationale: These measures aim to prevent complications in transit.

recommendations.statement: Intubate and ventilate anyone requiring transfer to a neuroscience unit with a GCS score of 8 or less, as well as anyone meeting the indications in recommendation 1.8.8.

Intubate and ventilate immediately for coma with no command-following, speech or eye opening (GCS score of 8 or less); absent protective laryngeal reflexes; ventilatory insufficiency shown by PaO2 less than 13 kPa on oxygen or PaCO2 more than 6 kPa; or irregular breathing.

Intubate and ventilate before departure if consciousness is significantly worsening, defined as 1 or more points on the motor score even without coma, or if there are unstable facial skeletal fractures, substantial oral bleeding or seizures.

For anyone intubated, provide appropriate sedation, analgesia and a neuromuscular blocking drug. Target PaO2 of more than 13 kPa and PaCO2 of 4.5 kPa to 5.0 kPa, unless clinical or imaging evidence of raised intracranial pressure justifies more aggressive hyperventilation; increase inspired oxygen if hyperventilating. Maintain mean arterial pressure at 80 mmHg or more using fluids and vasopressors as indicated.
Allow families and carers as much practical access to the injured person during transfer as possible, and, where possible, let them discuss the reasons and process with a healthcare team member.

Apply the principles of recommendations 1.8.1 to 1.8.9 and 1.8.11 to people under 16, using the paediatric GCS modification for preverbal and non-verbal children; ventilate according to age-appropriate oxygen saturation and maintain age-appropriate blood pressure.

Ensure tertiary transfer provision follows the NHS England service specification for paediatric intensive care retrieval (transport) and the Paediatric Critical Care Society quality standards for critically ill or injured children.
Consider hidden extracranial injury in multiply injured people under 16 and do not transfer them to a service that cannot manage their other trauma.

Transfer people under 16 to a specialist neurosurgical unit using staff experienced in transporting critically ill people under 16 or according to local arrangements involving specialist paediatric retrieval teams.

Give families and carers as much practical access to their child during transfer as possible and, where possible, an opportunity to discuss the reason for transfer and how it works with a healthcare team member.

Admit after head injury for a new clinically important imaging abnormality; a post-imaging GCS score not returned to 15 or the pre-injury baseline; an indicated CT that cannot be performed within its required timeframe; ongoing concerning symptoms such as persistent vomiting, severe headache or seizures; or other clinical concerns such as intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism, cerebrospinal fluid leak or suspected continuing post-traumatic amnesia. An isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture is unlikely to be clinically important unless the person takes anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication. Also consider discharge-related factors such as available home supervision.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered that simple linear non-displaced fractures alone are generally unlikely to be clinically important and that anticoagulant or antiplatelet use alone was not sufficiently supported as an admission indication after negative imaging.

recommendations.statement: Recognise that general anaesthesia for CT may require some people to remain longer in a recovery setting.
Admit multiply injured people to the team trained to address their most severe and urgent condition.

Admit a person with head injury under a consultant-led team trained in its management and competent, as locally agreed with the neuroscience unit, in assessment, observation, imaging indications, inpatient care, transfer indications, discharge and follow up.
For concussion symptoms with normal brain imaging or no early-imaging indication, apply the admission criteria in recommendation 1.9.1 and consult the discharge-advice section.
recommendations.rationale: The committee found no evidence warranting a change to existing admission practice for people with concussion symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: Admission and observation of people with concussion symptoms

recommendations.statement: Remain alert to pituitary dysfunction after a head injury of any severity: it may appear immediately or after hours, weeks or months, with varied symptoms.
recommendations.rationale: The committee noted that severity and delayed or varied presentation can complicate recognition of hypopituitarism.

recommendations.statement: Consider investigations for hypopituitarism in hospitalised people with head injury and persistently abnormally low sodium or low blood pressure.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered persistent clinical or biochemical abnormalities useful triggers for investigation after admission.

recommendations.statement: In primary or community care, consider investigation or referral for hypopituitarism when compatible symptoms persist for weeks or months after head injury.
recommendations.rationale: Pituitary dysfunction may emerge weeks or months after injury.

recommendations.statement: Restrict inpatient observation for head injury to professionals competent in head injury assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: At a minimum, document GCS score, pupil size and response, limb movement, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and blood oxygen saturation during inpatient head injury observation.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: Record observations half-hourly until GCS reaches 15. For a person with GCS score of 15, starting after initial emergency department assessment, observe at least half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: If a person with GCS score of 15 deteriorates after the initial 2-hour period, resume half-hourly checks and repeat the original observation-frequency schedule.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: Have a supervising doctor urgently reassess head injury when there is agitation or abnormal behaviour; a sustained drop of 1 point in GCS for at least 30 minutes, especially in motor response; a drop of 3 or more points in eye opening or verbal response, or 2 or more points in motor response; severe or worsening headache or persistent vomiting; or new or evolving neurological signs, including unequal pupils or asymmetric limb or facial movement.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: Where immediately possible, have another staff member competent in observation confirm suspected deterioration before calling the supervising doctor; if a second observer is unavailable, contact the doctor without awaiting confirmation.
recommendations.rationale: Confirmation aims to reduce variation between observers and unnecessary referrals.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: If deterioration described in recommendation 1.9.13 is confirmed, consider immediate CT, reassess clinical status and manage accordingly.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: If CT was normal but GCS has not reached 15 after 24 hours of observation, consider another CT or MRI and discuss imaging with radiology.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of people who are admitted

recommendations.statement: Observe babies and children under 5 with head injury only in units with staff experienced in observing that age group; ordinary paediatric observation settings can be used when staff have the requisite experience.
recommendations.rationale: Observation in babies and children under 5 is difficult.
recommendations.source_heading: Observation of babies and children under 5

recommendations.statement: Train all staff caring for admitted people undergoing head injury observation in the observations covered by recommendations 1.9.10 to 1.9.14 and in observing babies and children under 5.
Make dedicated training in observation and record-keeping available to relevant staff to establish and maintain competence, including specific training for observing people under 16.

When history and examination do not indicate CT and there is no suspected clinically important traumatic brain injury, discharge if there are no other admission factors, such as intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism or cerebrospinal fluid leak, and suitable community support and subsequent care, such as competent home supervision, are available.

After normal head imaging and with low risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury, transfer to the community only when GCS has returned to 15 or pre-injury baseline, no other admission factors are present, and adequate community support and subsequent care, such as competent home supervision, are available.

After normal cervical spine imaging, community transfer is appropriate when GCS is 15, clinical examination is normal, no other admission factors are present, and appropriate community support and subsequent care, such as competent home supervision, are available.

Do not discharge someone with head injury until GCS is 15; for preverbal or non-verbal children, require normal consciousness on paediatric GCS, and for people with pre-injury cognitive impairment, require return to the documented pre-injury GCS.

Send someone with any degree of head injury home only if a suitable person can supervise them there. If there is no home carer, discharge only once suitable supervision has been arranged or the risk of late complications is considered negligible.

Provide supervision and monitoring for people with pre-injury cognitive impairment, such as dementia or a learning disability, and for those returning to custody; establish a plan for responding to deterioration.
recommendations.rationale: Pre-existing cognitive impairment may make early symptoms of a delayed intracranial bleed harder to recognise or report; monitoring is also important in custodial settings.

recommendations.statement: A person admitted after head injury may be discharged once all significant signs and symptoms have resolved, provided suitable supervision is arranged at home, in custody or in continuing care.

Provide both spoken and printed discharge advice to anyone with head injury leaving an emergency department or observation ward, and to whoever will care for them afterwards, such as family, carers, social workers or custodial staff; provide information accessibly in line with the relevant NICE guidance.

Ensure age-appropriate printed advice for the injured person and their family or carers describes injury type and severity; factors requiring return to the emergency department; the need for a responsible adult to stay for the first 24 hours after injury; recovery, including possible later problems despite apparent early improvement; contacts for delayed complications; return to school, work, sport, driving and other activities; and support organisations.
When someone who attended the emergency department intoxicated with drugs or alcohol is ready for discharge, offer information and advice about substance misuse.
Explain to the injured person and their family or carers that symptoms may persist or arise later, and identify whom to contact for continuing difficulties.

Within 48 hours of discharge after an emergency department attendance for head injury, write to the person's GP with clinical history and examination details; also share the letter with health visitors for preschool children and school nurses for school-age children and young people. Where appropriate, give a copy to the injured person and their family or carers, custodial staff or social worker.
When appropriate, refer a person with head injury for assessment of its causes and management of contributing factors, such as falls assessment or safeguarding services.
recommendations.rationale: Some injured people remain at increased risk of further injury and may need access to preventive services.

recommendations.statement: Consider referral for persistent problems to a clinician trained in assessing and managing traumatic brain injury consequences, such as a neurologist, neuropsychologist, clinical psychologist, neurosurgeon or endocrinologist, or a multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation team.
recommendations.rationale: Persistent physical, sensory, motor, cognitive, emotional or hormonal problems can occur even without hospital admission or with normal initial imaging.

recommendations.statement: Consider additional endocrinology investigations after discharge for a person whose symptoms remain compatible with hypopituitarism or whose recovery is not as expected.
recommendations.rationale: Symptoms of hypopituitarism may be nonspecific or have other causes, making diagnosis difficult.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses assessment and early care after head injury in babies, children, young people and adults. Its aim is to match care to injury severity, including direct specialist referral when needed. Related NICE guidance on major trauma: service delivery addresses prehospital triage, transfer, pre-alerts, reception at trauma services, documentation, monitoring, audit and access to major trauma care. The intended readers are healthcare professionals, people with head injuries and their families or carers, and commissioners and providers.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: People should participate in informed decisions about their care. In this guideline, head injury means trauma to the head other than superficial facial injury; it includes closed and penetrating injuries. Babies are under 1 year, while children and young people are 1 year to under 16 years. NICE guidance on using recommendation wording explains how strength or certainty is expressed.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Decision making and mental capacity
document_sections.content: For collaborative decisions about treatment and care, consult NICE's guideline on shared decision making. For decisions involving people 16 and over who may lack capacity, now or later, including advance care plans, consult NICE's guideline on decision making and mental capacity. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Pre-hospital assessment, advice and referral to hospital
document_sections.content: Public health materials and non-medical advisers should encourage anyone concerned about their own or another person's head injury to obtain immediate medical advice, whatever its apparent severity. [2003]

document_sections.heading: Remote advice services
document_sections.content: Remote advisers should arrange emergency ambulance transport to an emergency department after head injury if the person is unconscious or not fully conscious, has had a focal neurological deficit or seizure since injury, has a suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating injury, has sustained a high-energy injury, or cannot otherwise reach the emergency department safely. [2003, amended 2007, 2014 and 2023] They should refer a person to an emergency department after injury if there has been recovered loss of consciousness; pre- or post-injury amnesia; persistent headache; any vomiting; previous brain surgery; a history of bleeding or clotting disorders; current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment except aspirin monotherapy; current intoxication with drugs or alcohol; safeguarding concerns; altered behaviour or irritability, particularly in babies and children under 5; or continuing diagnostic concern from helpline staff. Amnesia cannot be assessed in preverbal children and is unlikely to be assessable in children under 5. [2003, amended 2014 and 2023]

document_sections.heading: Community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department
document_sections.content: Community services and inpatient units without emergency departments should refer a person with head injury to an emergency department, using an ambulance if necessary, for an initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of less than 15; injury-related loss of consciousness; focal neurological deficit; suspected complex skull fracture or penetrating injury; pre- or post-injury amnesia; persistent headache; any vomiting; seizure; previous brain surgery; high-energy injury; a history of bleeding or clotting disorders; current anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment except aspirin monotherapy; intoxication; safeguarding concerns; or persisting professional concern about diagnosis. Amnesia assessment is not possible in preverbal children and is unlikely to be possible under 5. For children 12 years or under, clinical judgement should inform whether vomiting warrants referral. [2003, amended 2007, 2014 and 2023] When none of those risk factors applies, consider emergency department referral according to severity if there is behavioural change or irritability, especially under 5; concerning visible head trauma; nobody to observe the person at home; or continuing concern from the person, family or carer. [2003, amended 2014 and 2023]

document_sections.heading: Transport to hospital from community health services and inpatient units without an emergency department
document_sections.content: A competent adult should accompany people referred from community services during travel to the emergency department. [2003] The referring professional should decide whether the clinical condition requires an ambulance; if not, travel by car or public transport is suitable when the person is accompanied. The professional should telephone the receiving hospital before transfer and, for non-emergency transfer, provide a letter describing signs and symptoms. [2003]

document_sections.heading: Training in risk assessment
document_sections.content: Train GPs, nurse practitioners, dentists and ambulance crews when necessary so they can identify the presence or absence of the referral risk factors specified for community services and inpatient units without an emergency department. [2003, amended 2007]

document_sections.heading: Glasgow Coma Scale
document_sections.content: Monitoring and communication should use the 3 separate GCS responses: for example, a total of 13 comprising eye opening 4, verbal response 4 and motor response 5 is recorded E4, V4, M5. State the total as a score out of 15, for example, 13 out of 15, and include the component scores in every record and communication. The paediatric GCS should offer 'grimace' instead of the verbal response for preverbal children. Where a person's baseline before injury may have been below 15, including with dementia, chronic neurological disease or learning disability, establish and account for that baseline where possible. [2003] [2014]

document_sections.heading: Initial assessment and care
document_sections.content: For people 16 and over, initial assessment and management should follow clear, standard trauma principles reflected in the Advanced Trauma Life Support course or European Trauma course; International Trauma Life Support course; Pre-hospital Trauma Life Support course; Advanced Trauma Nurse Course; Trauma Nursing Core Course; and Joint Royal Colleges Ambulance Service Liaison Committee Clinical Practice Guidelines for Head Trauma. [2003, amended 2007] For people under 16, use principles from the Advanced Paediatric Life Support course or European Paediatric Life Support course, Pre-hospital Paediatric Life Support course and Paediatric Education for Pre-hospital Professionals course. [2003, amended 2007] Address the most immediate threat to life first and prevent additional harm; related NICE major trauma guidance covers volume resuscitation when traumatic brain injury accompanies haemorrhagic shock. Refer to NICE spinal injury guidance for indications and duration of full in-line immobilisation. [2003, amended 2007] Pre-alert the destination emergency department for a GCS score of 8 or less so experienced staff and imaging preparations are available. [2003] Treat pain effectively because pain may raise intracranial pressure; offer reassurance, splint fractured limbs and catheterise a full bladder when needed. Follow National Paediatric Neuroscience Benchmarking Group practice for observing and recording paediatric coma. [2007, amended 2014] [2003]

document_sections.heading: Transport to hospital
document_sections.content: Take a person with head injury directly to an age-appropriate major trauma centre or trauma unit equipped for further resuscitation, investigation and initial treatment of multiple injuries. NICE guidance on major trauma: service delivery covers care for major trauma. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Training for ambulance crews and paramedics
document_sections.content: Ambulance crews and paramedics should be trained fully in adult and paediatric GCS versions and the derived score. They should also be trained to safeguard vulnerable people 16 and over and people under 16, recording concerns and communicating them verbally to emergency department staff. [2003] [2003, amended 2014]

document_sections.heading: Tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: For a head injury with GCS score of 12 or less and no suspected active extracranial bleeding, consider an intravenous bolus of tranexamic acid: 2 g for people 16 and over, or 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 2 g) for people under 16. Give it as early as possible within 2 hours of injury, before imaging, in hospital or prehospital care. These uses were off-label in March 2023. If extracranial bleeding is suspected or confirmed, consult NICE's major trauma recommendations on haemostatic agents. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Direct access from the community to imaging
document_sections.content: Do not send someone with head injury directly from a community setting for neuroimaging. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Assessment in the emergency department
document_sections.content: For every emergency department arrival, stabilise airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) before addressing other injuries. Do not attribute reduced consciousness to intoxication until important traumatic brain injury has been excluded. Clinicians assessing head injury should be able to identify the listed risk factors for head and cervical spine CT, with training provided as necessary. A trained staff member should assess impaired consciousness, defined here as GCS less than 15, immediately. Consult the tranexamic acid recommendations for GCS 12 or less. For GCS 8 or less, involve an appropriately trained advanced-airway clinician early to assist resuscitation. [2003] [2023] A trained staff member should assess each emergency department presentation with head injury within a maximum of 15 minutes of hospital arrival, including initial categorisation of risk for clinically important brain or cervical spine injury. High-risk patients need full examination to identify imaging requirements for the head, cervical spine or other sites. Those initially classified as low risk need reassessment by an emergency department clinician. Base final imaging decisions on the relevant age-specific criteria after discussion with radiology. Reassess anyone returning with persistent symptoms from the original injury, discuss the case with a senior clinician experienced in head injury and consider CT. Treat pain to help avert raised intracranial pressure, with reassurance, fracture splinting and bladder catheterisation when required. Consider or suspect abuse, neglect or other safeguarding concerns as a possible cause or contributor. [2003, amended 2007] [2003, amended 2007 and 2023] [2003, amended 2023] [2007] [2023] Include a safeguarding-trained clinician in the initial assessment; document concerns and follow age-appropriate local safeguarding procedures. Use a consistent standard head-injury proforma across hospital departments for assessment and observation, with a separate form for people under 16 and space for extra details such as possible non-accidental injury. [2003, amended 2014] [2003, amended 2007]

document_sections.heading: Involving the neurosurgical department
