document_sections.content: Discuss new, surgically significant imaging abnormalities with a neurosurgeon; local neurosurgical centres and referring hospitals should agree on the meaning of surgically significant findings and referral arrangements. [2003, amended 2014] Irrespective of imaging, seek neurosurgical discussion for persistent coma after initial resuscitation (GCS 8 or less), otherwise unexplained confusion lasting more than 4 hours, a declining GCS after admission, progressive focal neurological signs, seizure without complete recovery, definite or suspected penetrating injury, or cerebrospinal fluid leak. Give particular attention to worsening motor response. [2003]

document_sections.heading: 1.5 Investigating clinically important traumatic brain injuries
document_sections.content: Head CT is the principal initial investigation for an acute clinically important traumatic brain injury. MRI should not be the primary investigation for this purpose because of safety, logistical and resource issues, although it can sometimes add prognostic information. For MRI, provide suitable head-injury monitoring equipment and ensure personnel understand scanner-related hazards and precautions. Do not use plain skull X-rays to diagnose important traumatic brain injury without first discussing the case with a neuroscience unit; a skeletal survey may nevertheless be required for a person under 16 with suspected non-accidental injury. If CT is indicated but unavailable at the presenting hospital, arrange transfer to a suitable hospital, and trauma networks should enable such transfers. Minimise head and cervical spine imaging radiation doses while preserving sufficient image quality and anatomical coverage. [2003] [2007] [2007, amended 2023]

document_sections.heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan
document_sections.content: The age-specific criteria below distinguish findings that require CT within 1 hour from circumstances calling for later imaging, observation or consideration of CT. A provisional written radiology report should be available within 1 hour of CT. [2014]

document_sections.heading: People 16 and over
document_sections.content: Perform head CT within 1 hour of recognising any of these findings after head injury: GCS 12 or less at initial emergency department assessment; GCS less than 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; basal skull fracture signs, including haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from an ear or the nose, or Battle's sign; post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; or more than 1 vomiting episode. [2023] If there has been loss of consciousness or amnesia, perform head CT within 8 hours of injury, or within the hour for presentation more than 8 hours after injury, if there is age 65 or over; a current bleeding or clotting disorder; a dangerous mechanism involving a pedestrian or cyclist struck by a motor vehicle, occupant ejection or fall from more than 1 m or 5 stairs; or retrograde amnesia lasting more than 30 minutes immediately before the injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: People under 16
document_sections.content: Perform head CT within 1 hour of identifying suspected non-accidental injury; post-traumatic seizure; initial emergency department GCS less than 14, or paediatric GCS less than 15 for a baby under 1 year; GCS less than 15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture or tense fontanelle; basal skull fracture signs, including haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the ear or nose, or Battle's sign; focal neurological deficit; or, in a baby under 1 year, a head bruise, swelling or laceration exceeding 5 cm. [2023] CT is also required within 1 hour of recognising more than 1 of the following: witnessed unconsciousness lasting more than 5 minutes; abnormal drowsiness; 3 or more distinct vomiting episodes; a dangerous mechanism involving a high-speed road traffic accident as pedestrian, cyclist or vehicle occupant, a fall from more than 3 m, or a high-speed projectile or other object; anterograde or retrograde amnesia exceeding 5 minutes; or a current bleeding or clotting disorder. Amnesia is unassessable in preverbal children and unlikely to be assessable under 5. [2023] If only 1 of these latter factors applies, observe for a minimum of 4 hours from injury; obtain head CT within 1 hour if GCS falls below 15, vomiting recurs or another episode of abnormal drowsiness occurs. Without these developments, use clinical judgement on whether observation should continue longer. [2023]

document_sections.heading: People taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication
document_sections.content: When no other head-CT indication exists, consider CT for a person taking anticoagulants—including vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin or low molecular weight heparins—or antiplatelets other than aspirin monotherapy. Consider imaging within 8 hours of injury, including when assessment is difficult or return after deterioration is doubtful, or within the hour if presentation occurs more than 8 hours after injury. For reversal advice in traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, the guideline points to NICE blood transfusion guidance for vitamin K antagonists and MHRA safety advice for DOACs. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Timing of radiology report
document_sections.content: Provide a provisional report in writing within 1 hour after CT. [2014]

document_sections.heading: Investigation to predict post-concussion syndrome
document_sections.content: For possible post-concussion syndrome, the guideline directs readers to its follow-up recommendation on considering referral for persistent problems. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Assessing range of movement in the neck
document_sections.content: Before imaging, assess neck movement in a person with head injury and suspected cervical injury only when high-risk factors are absent and at least 1 low-risk feature is present: a simple rear-end vehicle collision, comfort while sitting, walking at some point since injury, absence of midline cervical tenderness, or delayed onset of neck pain. [2014]

document_sections.heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people 16 and over
document_sections.content: After head injury, including delayed presentation, obtain cervical spine CT within 1 hour of identifying any high-risk factor: initial GCS 12 or less; intubation; urgent need for a definitive cervical diagnosis, such as before manipulation during surgery or anaesthesia; blunt polytrauma affecting the head and chest, abdomen or pelvis in an alert, stable person; or suspected cervical spine injury accompanied by age 65 or over, a dangerous mechanism, focal peripheral neurological deficit, or limb paraesthesia. Dangerous mechanisms comprise falls from more than 1 m or 5 stairs, axial head loading such as diving, high-speed motor vehicle collision, vehicle rollover, ejection, a motorised recreational vehicle accident or bicycle collision. [2023] With neck pain or tenderness but no high-risk indication, obtain CT within 1 hour if neck-movement assessment is considered unsafe, if safe assessment finds inability to rotate actively 45 degrees to both left and right, or if a condition such as axial spondyloarthritis predisposes to cervical injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Criteria for doing a CT cervical spine scan in people under 16
document_sections.content: After head injury, including delayed presentation, perform cervical CT only for initial GCS 12 or less; intubation; focal peripheral neurological signs; upper- or lower-limb paraesthesia; urgent need for a definitive cervical injury diagnosis; scanning other body regions for head injury or multisystem trauma together with suspected cervical injury; strong clinical suspicion despite normal X-rays; technically inadequate or difficult X-rays; or significant bony injury on plain X-rays. Complete CT within 1 hour of identifying the factor. [2023] For neck pain or tenderness without a CT indication, obtain 3-view cervical X-rays before assessing neck movement if there is a dangerous mechanism, movement assessment cannot safely be undertaken, or a predisposing condition such as collagen vascular disease, osteogenesis imperfecta or axial spondyloarthritis exists. Dangerous mechanisms include falls from more than 1 m or 5 stairs, axial loading such as diving, high-speed motor collision, rollover, ejection, a motorised recreational vehicle accident or bicycle collision. Obtain and have a trained clinician review X-rays within 1 hour of identifying the factor. [2023] If movement assessment is safe but active rotation of 45 degrees to the left and right is impossible, obtain 3-view cervical X-rays within 1 hour and have a trained clinician interpret them. A peg view may be omitted if the person cannot understand instructions or open their mouth. [2014]

document_sections.heading: Imaging investigations
document_sections.content: Cervical imaging reports should draw on high-resolution original data and multiplanar reconstructions covering the entire cervical spine. Add MRI to CT for neurological symptoms or signs suggesting cervical injury. Use CT or MRI angiography of neck vessels when vascular injury is suspected, for example because of vertebral malalignment, a high-risk fracture involving complex or high-grade facial injury or a skull-base fracture likely to involve the internal carotid or vertebral artery, or posterior circulation syndrome. Consider MRI when clinical findings or CT suggest ligament or disc injury. [2003, amended 2014 and 2023] [2003]

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Information and support for families and carers
document_sections.content: Staff should introduce themselves to relatives or carers and briefly explain their activities. Information supplied to families and carers should describe the injury and likely route of care. Staff should choose how best to inform people under 16 about possible complex, lasting changes in an injured parent or sibling; patient-group materials may help. Encourage family and carers to talk with and touch the injured person if appropriate, without making them feel obliged to remain at the bedside for long periods; encourage regular breaks if they stay. Display leaflets or contact information for local and national patient support organisations. [2003] [2003, amended 2014] [2003, amended 2007]

document_sections.heading: Transfer of people 16 and over
document_sections.content: Referring hospitals, neuroscience units and ambulance services should agree local transfer guidance for severe traumatic brain injury. Transfer would benefit people with serious injury and GCS 8 or less irrespective of whether surgery is needed; where a non-surgical transfer is impossible, continued management liaison with the neuroscience unit is essential. [2003, amended 2007] For multiple injuries, consider hidden extracranial trauma and avoid transfer to a service unable to treat other injuries. Designate consultants at both referring and neuroscience hospitals to arrange transfer, communication and reception. Emergency transfers should be accompanied by personnel experienced and trained in acute traumatic brain injury transfer, familiar with injury pathophysiology, medicines, equipment and ambulance or helicopter work; they should have a dedicated trained assistant, suitable clothing, medical indemnity and personal accident insurance. Appropriate clinical personnel should accompany non-emergency transfers. Provide a way to communicate changes in clinical status between the transfer team, its base hospital and the neurosurgical unit. [2007] [2003] [2003, amended 2007] [2003, amended 2014] Complete initial resuscitation and stabilisation and establish comprehensive monitoring before travel, despite urgency. Do not transport a person with persistent hypotension after resuscitation until its cause is identified and the person is stable. Intubate and ventilate those needing neuroscience transfer with GCS 8 or less and those meeting the further indications. Immediate intubation and ventilation are indicated for coma—failure to obey commands, speak and open eyes, with GCS 8 or less—loss of protective laryngeal reflexes, respiratory insufficiency shown by PaO2 less than 13 kPa on oxygen or PaCO2 more than 6 kPa, or irregular breathing. [2003, amended 2007] [2003] Before departure, intubate and ventilate for a substantially declining level of consciousness, defined as 1 or more points on the motor score even without coma, unstable facial fractures, copious oral bleeding or seizures. An intubated person should receive suitable sedation, analgesia and a neuromuscular blocking drug. Target PaO2 more than 13 kPa and PaCO2 4.5 kPa to 5.0 kPa, except that clinical or imaging evidence of raised intracranial pressure justifies stronger hyperventilation; if hyperventilating, increase inspired oxygen. Maintain mean arterial pressure at 80 mmHg or more with fluids and vasopressors when indicated. Allow families and carers as much access during transfer as feasible and, where possible, an explanation of its reasons and process. [2003, amended 2007] [2003, amended 2014]

document_sections.heading: Transfer of people under 16
document_sections.content: Apply the principles of recommendations 1.8.1 to 1.8.9 and 1.8.11, originally written for people 16 and over, to people under 16, using paediatric GCS modifications for preverbal or non-verbal children. Ventilation should meet age-appropriate oxygen saturation targets and blood pressure should be maintained at an age-appropriate level. Tertiary transfers should follow the NHS England paediatric intensive care retrieval service specification and Paediatric Critical Care Society quality standards. For multiple injuries, consider hidden extracranial injury and avoid transfer to services unable to treat other trauma. Specialist neurosurgical transfer should be undertaken by staff experienced with critically ill people under 16 or according to local arrangements involving specialist paediatric retrieval teams. Give relatives and carers as much feasible access to their child during transfer and, if possible, an explanation of why and how transfer occurs. [2003, amended 2023] [2003] [2007] [2003, amended 2014]

document_sections.heading: 1.9 Admission and observation
document_sections.content: Admit after head injury for newly identified clinically important imaging abnormalities; GCS not returned to 15 or the pre-injury baseline after imaging, irrespective of imaging findings; an indicated CT that cannot be completed in the required interval owing to scanner unavailability or inadequate cooperation; persistent concerning symptoms, such as vomiting, severe headache or seizure; or other clinical concerns, including intoxication, additional injury, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism, cerebrospinal fluid leak or suspected continuing post-traumatic amnesia. An isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture is unlikely to be clinically important unless the person takes anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication. Consider home supervision when planning discharge. [2003, amended 2023] General anaesthesia for CT may require longer recovery-setting care. Multiple-injury admissions should be under the team qualified to address the most urgent and severe problem. Head-injury admissions should be led by a consultant trained in the condition, whose team meets locally agreed neuroscience-unit competencies in assessment, observation, imaging indications, inpatient care, neuroscience transfer, discharge and follow-up. [2003, amended 2007] [2003]

document_sections.heading: Admission and observation of people with concussion symptoms
document_sections.content: For concussion symptoms with normal brain imaging or no indication for early imaging, use the same admission criteria specified for head injury generally and consult the discharge-advice recommendations. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Early diagnosis of hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: Pituitary dysfunction can follow a head injury of any severity and may emerge immediately or after hours, weeks or months; possible symptoms vary. Consider hypopituitarism investigations for an admitted person with persistently low sodium or blood pressure. In primary or community care, consider investigations or referral for persistent compatible symptoms in the weeks or months after head injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Observation of people who are admitted
document_sections.content: Only personnel competent in head-injury assessment should undertake inpatient observation. At minimum, document GCS, pupil size and reactions, limb movements, breathing rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and oxygen saturation. Record observations every half-hour until GCS reaches 15. After initial emergency department assessment, observe someone with GCS 15 at least half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1 hourly for 4 hours, then 2 hourly. If such a person deteriorates at any point after the initial 2-hour period, return to half-hourly observation and repeat the original schedule. [2003] A supervising doctor should urgently reassess agitation or unusual behaviour; a GCS reduction of 1 point sustained for at least 30 minutes, especially in motor response; a fall of 3 or more points in eye opening or verbal response, or 2 or more in motor response; severe or worsening headache or persistent vomiting; or emerging or changing neurological findings, including unequal pupils or asymmetric facial or limb movements. If possible, have another observation-competent staff member promptly verify deterioration before contacting the doctor, reducing observer variation and unnecessary referral; if immediate verification is unavailable, contact the doctor without waiting. Once such a change is confirmed, consider immediate CT, reassess clinically and manage accordingly. If CT was normal but GCS remains below 15 after 24 hours of observation, consider another CT or MRI after discussion with radiology. [2003, amended 2007] [2003]

document_sections.heading: Observation of babies and children under 5
document_sections.content: Because observation is difficult in babies and children under 5, it should be undertaken only in units with staff experienced in observing head injuries in this age group. A standard paediatric observation setting is acceptable if its staff have that experience. [2003]

document_sections.heading: Training in observation
document_sections.content: Staff observing admitted patients should be trained in the specified neurological assessments, observation frequency, detection and verification of deterioration, and requirements for babies and children under 5. Provide dedicated opportunities to gain and maintain recording and observation skills; people under 16 require specific training. [2003]

document_sections.heading: 1.10 Discharge and follow up
document_sections.content: If history and examination do not indicate CT and important traumatic brain injury is not suspected, discharge is appropriate only without another admission reason and with adequate community support, such as competent home supervision. After normal head imaging and with low risk of important traumatic brain injury, community transfer additionally requires GCS 15 or the pre-injury baseline. After normal cervical imaging, transfer requires GCS 15, a normal clinical examination, no other admission reason and suitable support. Potential admission reasons include intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism or cerebrospinal fluid leak. [2003] Do not discharge until GCS reaches 15, normal consciousness is established through paediatric GCS in preverbal or non-verbal children, or the documented pre-injury GCS is regained in someone with prior cognitive impairment. Send someone home only when suitable supervision is available; without a carer, discharge only if alternative supervision is arranged or late-complication risk is judged negligible. [2003]

document_sections.heading: People with pre-injury cognitive impairment
document_sections.content: Arrange supervision and monitoring after discharge for people with pre-injury cognitive impairment, such as dementia or a learning disability, and for those returning to custody. Ensure a response plan exists if deterioration appears. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Discharge after observation
document_sections.content: A person admitted after head injury may leave once all significant symptoms and signs have resolved, provided suitable supervision is available at home, in custody or in ongoing care. [2003, amended 2023]

document_sections.heading: Discharge advice
document_sections.content: Provide both spoken and printed advice to anyone discharged from an emergency department or observation ward after head injury, irrespective of severity, and to whoever will care for them, including family, carers, social workers or custodial personnel; make information accessible in line with related NICE guidance. [2014, amended 2023] Age-appropriate written advice should explain injury type and severity, warning factors requiring return to the emergency department, the need for a responsible adult to remain with the person for the first 24 hours after injury, recovery and the possibility of later difficulties despite apparently rapid improvement, community and hospital contacts for delayed complications, return to school, work, sport and driving, and support organisations. [2014] At discharge, offer advice about alcohol or drug misuse to people who presented intoxicated. Explain possible persistent or delayed symptoms and whom to contact. Send the GP a letter describing history and examination within 48 hours of discharge after any emergency department attendance for head injury; also share it with health visitors for preschool children or school nurses for school-age children and young people, and give other parties a copy when appropriate. [2003] [2014]

document_sections.heading: Follow up
document_sections.content: Refer for assessment of injury causes and management of contributing factors when appropriate, including falls assessment or safeguarding services. Consider referral for persistent problems to someone trained to assess and manage consequences of traumatic brain injury, such as a neurologist, neuropsychologist, clinical psychologist, neurosurgeon, endocrinologist or multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation team. [2023] [2003, amended 2023]

document_sections.heading: Investigations for hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: After discharge for head injury, consider additional endocrinology investigations if symptoms compatible with hypopituitarism persist or recovery is not proceeding as expected. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Closed head injury
document_sections.content: A closed injury may result from direct impact or indirect force such as shaking or deceleration without an object penetrating skull or brain tissue. It can stretch, shear or tear nerves at the brain base and cause intracranial or surrounding blood clots or brain swelling. A skull fracture can occur without creating a direct brain-to-outside connection.

document_sections.heading: Focal neurological deficit
document_sections.content: This denotes a neurological difficulty confined to a body region or function. Examples are impaired comprehension, speech, reading or writing; reduced sensation; balance loss; weakness; altered vision; nystagmus; abnormal reflexes; walking difficulties; and amnesia after injury.

document_sections.heading: Glasgow Coma Scale
document_sections.content: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) provides an early, standardised assessment of brain dysfunction and injury seriousness in relation to outcome. Eye opening, verbal response and motor response receive independent numerical assessments, which are added to produce a total from 3 for no response in any domain to 15 for no responsiveness deficit. Mild traumatic brain injury corresponds to GCS 13 to 15, moderate to 9 to 12, and severe to 8 or less.

document_sections.heading: High-energy head injury
document_sections.content: Examples include a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, vehicle occupant ejection, a fall of more than 1 m or more than 5 stairs, diving, a high-speed motor vehicle collision, vehicle rollover, a motorised recreational vehicle accident, a bicycle collision or another potentially high-energy mechanism.

document_sections.heading: Hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: Reduced pituitary activity can produce adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency, with weakness, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia or anaemia; growth hormone deficiency, with reduced energy, low mood, neuropsychiatric or cognitive symptoms, less lean mass, more fat mass, metabolic changes or reduced exercise capacity; sex-hormone deficiency, with late puberty, hot flushes, fatigue, loss of body hair, reduced libido, irregular periods, erectile dysfunction or lower fertility; thyroid-stimulating hormone deficiency, with slow growth, fatigue, lethargy, cold intolerance or weight gain; and vasopressin deficiency, with polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia or incontinence.

document_sections.heading: Isolated simple linear non-displaced skull fracture
document_sections.content: This is a single linear fracture without inward or outward displacement, multiple fracture lines, or involvement or crossing of normal skull sutures.

document_sections.heading: Paraesthesia
document_sections.content: This means pins and needles or a prickling, tingling or itching sensation anywhere in the body.

document_sections.heading: Penetrating head injury
document_sections.content: An object passes through the scalp and skull into the brain or its covering.

document_sections.heading: Post-concussion syndrome
document_sections.content: Post-concussion syndrome, also termed post-concussion symptoms, can follow head injury of any severity and is insufficiently recognised after mild injury. Evidence review F uses the syndrome terminology; evidence review J uses 'concussion'. Possible sensory and motor symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, blurred or double vision and other altered visual experiences, problems processing visual information, prolonged sleep or difficulty remaining awake, chronic fatigue, sensitivity to noise or bright light, impaired balance, coordination or mobility with possible falls or additional injury, and speech difficulties. Cognitive features include 'brain fog' despite GCS 15, problems finding words or numbers, slowed responses, short-term memory or concentration difficulties, difficulty processing conversations or text, impaired organisation, planning or multitasking, amnesia, and altered spatial awareness or proprioception. Emotional features include unusual laughing or crying, irritability, depression and anxiety. In children under 5, additional possible features are more crying or irritability, altered feeding or sleep, reduced interest in people or objects, and listlessness.

document_sections.heading: Signs of a complex skull fracture or penetrating head injury
document_sections.content: Possible signs of a basal, open or depressed fracture or penetrating injury include clear discharge from an ear or the nose, a black eye without local surrounding injury, bleeding from 1 or both ears, bruising behind 1 or both ears, signs of penetration, or scalp or skull trauma that concerns the professional.

document_sections.heading: Traumatic brain injury
document_sections.content: An external force causes changed brain function or other evidence of brain pathology.

document_sections.heading: 1 Indications for admission in people with a mild head injury and a confirmed abnormality on a CT scan
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research into admission criteria and clinical decision rules for a confirmed CT abnormality with GCS 13 to 15, described as mild head injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 2 Using biomarkers for predicting acute post-traumatic brain injury complications
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research into the diagnostic accuracy of brain injury biomarkers for acute complications after traumatic brain injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 3 Indications for imaging for people with a history of recurrent head injuries
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research into intracranial injury risk after recurrent head injuries, including sports injuries and falls, when there is no other CT indication. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 4 Risk of bleeding for people with a pre-injury coagulopathy
document_sections.content: The committee calls for research into intracranial bleeding, including bleeding associated with clinical decline, after head injury in people with pre-injury coagulopathy, including liver failure, haemophilia and anticoagulant or antiplatelet use. Groups of interest are people with GCS 15 at 2 hours and medium-risk bleeding factors; those with loss of consciousness or amnesia but no additional factors, meaning under 65, a low-energy transfer injury and retrograde amnesia shorter than 30 minutes; and those without loss of consciousness or amnesia. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 5 Indications for imaging for people with a pre-injury cognitive impairment
document_sections.content: Research is sought on imaging selection at any age after a low-energy fall with suspected pre-injury cognitive impairment when loss of consciousness or amnesia cannot readily be assessed or baseline GCS is not 15. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 6 Transport to a neuroscience centre
document_sections.content: The committee seeks research on clinical and cost effectiveness of prehospital transport to a distant specialist neuroscience centre instead of a nearer non-specialist unit. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 7 Tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: Research is requested on clinical and cost effectiveness of tranexamic acid before imaging for presentation within 2 hours of head injury, GCS 13 to 15 and high-risk features for intracranial bleeding. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 8 Indications for selecting people for imaging when they present more than 24 hours after a head injury
document_sections.content: The committee seeks criteria for head CT or MRI in people of any age presenting more than 24 hours after injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 9 Using biomarkers and MRI for predicting post-concussion syndrome
document_sections.content: The proposed research would determine the prognostic accuracy of brain injury biomarkers or MRI for post-concussion syndrome. [2023]

document_sections.heading: 10 Timing of testing for hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: The committee requests research into when to investigate hypopituitarism after head injury. [2023]

document_sections.heading: Decision making and mental capacity
document_sections.content: The committee emphasised including injured people and their relatives or carers in care and emergency-referral decisions, respecting advance care plans and addressing decisions where capacity may be absent now or in the future. It did not expect changes in practice or services.

document_sections.heading: Transport to hospital
document_sections.content: The committee identified 1 randomised controlled trial (RCT) and 1 retrospective cohort study comparing transport to a specialist neuroscience centre with transport to a nearer non-specialist acute hospital or general hospital emergency department. Participants were 16 and over; there was no evidence for people under 16. The RCT suggested a possible mortality benefit from non-specialist general-hospital transfer, but with uncertainty. The cohort study suggested no difference in survival benefit between its 2 groups. The committee considered evidence of a possible specialist-centre benefit for some outcomes limited and uncertain, and found no compelling reason to alter practice. RCT data were gathered in 2012, when UK trauma care was reorganised; those data do not reflect the later system with more consultants, faster CT and rehabilitation. The committee therefore sought further research and did not expect a practice or service change.

document_sections.heading: Tranexamic acid
document_sections.content: For people 16 and over, the committee found 2 RCTs of tranexamic acid without suspected extracranial bleeding: 1 prehospital and 1 hospital-based. No evidence directly addressed people under 16, although 1 trial included a few people aged 15 and 16. In the prehospital trial, a single 2 g bolus within 2 hours suggested lower all-cause mortality at 28 days and 6 months for moderate or severe traumatic brain injury. It showed no clinically important difference from placebo in hospital-free days at 28 days, disability at discharge or 6 months measured as Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended more than 4, or serious adverse events comprising myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis and stroke. In the hospital trial, a 1 g bolus within 3 hours followed by 1 g intravenously over 8 hours suggested reduced traumatic-brain-injury death at 28 days in combined mild or moderate groups. It suggested lower traumatic-brain-injury mortality at 28 days for severe injury in high-income countries but no such difference in low- and middle-income countries. Mortality results did not separate mild and moderate groups; correspondence with study authors indicated substantial uncertainty about effects in mild injury. Serious adverse events and disability rating scale scores did not differ clinically importantly from placebo across the mixed mild, moderate and severe group and income settings. Despite clinical uncertainty, the committee judged mortality benefits and very few adverse events sufficient to consider a 2 g intravenous bolus within 2 hours and before imaging for moderate or severe injury at age 16 and over; it considered this dose safest and most effective. Its economic model assessed severity groups separately, using principally the prehospital trial because moderate data were separate and earlier administration showed greater benefit. With moderate injury, benefits exceeded costs in all scenarios; severe-injury cost effectiveness was more borderline, but modelling limitations led the committee to judge that benefits were likely to exceed costs. For people under 16, it extrapolated from adult trials and clinical expertise. A 15 mg/kg dose is used for extracranial injuries in NHS practice, whereas isolated-injury use is not widespread and doses vary from 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg. The committee related an adult 2 g dose and assumed 70 kg average adult weight to 30 mg/kg, concluding that 15 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg was appropriate. For mild injury, whether benefits exceed possible clotting risks remained unclear, prompting research. Increased paramedic use for isolated injury was anticipated, potentially improving survival and requiring additional treatment, rehabilitation and care resources.

document_sections.heading: Direct access from the community to imaging
document_sections.content: No evidence compared community-initiated head CT or MRI with usual care after suspected or confirmed head injury, including delayed presentation or residence in care settings. The committee noted that community imaging is mainly sought to exclude bleeding or reassure, and timing depends on acute injury versus post-concussion syndrome. In its experience, important traumatic brain injury within 24 hours or reduced GCS warrants hospital attendance. Community access, prompt reporting and interpretation of complex neuroradiology reports present difficulties during acute injury; consequently, it opposed direct community imaging referral. A few centres using such routes may need to refer through emergency departments instead.

document_sections.heading: Assessment in the emergency department
document_sections.content: The committee emphasised applying relevant safeguarding guidance when abuse or another safeguarding issue could contribute to head injury. It anticipated no change in practice or services.

document_sections.heading: Criteria for doing a CT head scan
document_sections.content: For people 16 and over, several diagnostic-accuracy studies but no diagnostic RCTs were identified. Most evidence was low or very low quality and concerned mild injury, usually GCS 13 to 15 but sometimes 14 to 15. Existing imaging recommendations largely derive from the Canadian CT Head Rule (CCHR), modified to improve sensitivity. Updated evidence suggested good sensitivity when CCHR is applied as intended but poor specificity, reflecting the priority given to very high sensitivity. Other rules had similar sensitivity but generally worse specificity than the CCHR high- and medium-risk rule; limited evidence suggested NEXUS 2 had comparable specificity. Only 1 study evaluated NICE's 2014 update, finding worse sensitivity than CCHR but better specificity than other rules. The committee considered reasons for those results unclear, including possible population differences, and judged the reported NICE sensitivity lower than clinical experience suggested. It considered evidence insufficient to change adult rules; economic evidence also identified CCHR as the most cost effective among assessed rules. For people under 16, existing rules largely follow CHALICE with modifications permitting observation before imaging in some cases. Updated CHALICE evidence showed good sensitivity for important injuries and neurosurgical outcomes. PECARN and CATCH-7 might have slightly better sensitivity, but CHALICE specificity was considerably better and its sensitivity remained over 90%. PECARN was considered less precise on timing and, alongside CATCH-7, applied to narrower populations. The committee found insufficient evidence to change widely used paediatric recommendations. It retained recommendations on current bleeding or clotting disorders, replacing wording referring to history because paediatric disorders can resolve and historical screening is an imperfect tool for emergency assessment. Cohort findings conflicted on whether anticoagulants or antiplatelets increase intracranial bleeding. The committee considered the evidence too weak to stop considering CT in otherwise low-risk anticoagulated patients; it changed automatic scanning to consideration and included antiplatelets except aspirin monotherapy. Risk assessment can encompass other injuries, home supervision, injury cause and further falls. With no risks and after shared decisions, low-risk patients might safely leave without CT and with usual advice; when risks exist, clinicians would image or admit for monitoring. Undetected bleeding was considered more likely to delay recovery than cause death, and surgery was considered less likely over 74 because of its risk-benefit balance. Existing practice performed CT within 8 hours in otherwise low-risk anticoagulated patients; antiplatelet imaging practices varied. The committee included antiplatelets other than aspirin monotherapy without restricting the category to named drugs and extrapolated the approach to presentation more than 8 hours after injury, with imaging within an hour of confirming relevant medication. Limited aspirin evidence and clinical experience suggested low haemorrhage risk, even with symptoms; aspirin monotherapy alone was not considered a reason for CT or admission after shared decisions. No evidence specifically addressed liver or coagulopathy disorders; practice varied, bleeding risk is elevated although some individuals tend to clot more, and acquired disorders are heterogeneous. Limited adult cohort evidence on low-energy falls linked standing-position falls, age over 70, reduced GCS, antiplatelets including aspirin, and neurological symptoms to intracranial bleeding, but not anticoagulants in that studied population; whether participants had prior cognitive impairment was unclear. Dementia can obscure or reduce reporting of symptoms, and no evidence addressed people under 16 with pre-injury impairment. No evidence addressed recurrent head injury; repetition, including through sport, could create cumulative risks. For presentations more than 24 hours after injury, 1 observational study suggested greater CT-detected injury risk in children under 2 with younger age, GCS less than 15 or presentation more than 24 hours after injury. There was no evidence for people 2 years or over; the committee extrapolated recommendations previously directed at presentation within 24 hours and sought research. Moving from 'offer' to 'consider' CT for anticoagulation alone could reduce scans, while inclusion of clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor could increase them; the net effect was uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Post-concussion syndrome
document_sections.content: The committee considered high specificity essential for biomarkers predicting post-concussion syndrome because only a small fraction of the large mild-injury population develops it and false positives would consume intervention or monitoring resources. Evidence was too limited to recommend fluid biomarkers or MRI for this prediction, and no prognostic test-and-treat comparison of clinical outcomes existed. For acute complications, some biomarker thresholds showed high sensitivity in diagnostic-accuracy studies, but specificity was insufficient across the evidence. Small samples gave imprecise estimates; assays, platforms, thresholds and measurement times varied, and accuracy differed widely even for the same biomarker. Most hospital presentations occur within 3 hours, the manufacturers' recommended optimal testing window, but many studies tested later. Given unnecessary CT radiation, particularly under 16, specificity mattered as much as sensitivity. The committee could not recommend biomarkers for acute complications after mild injury, although it considered them promising enough for research. Biomarkers were not routinely used in acute injury, MRI recommendations had not changed, and no practice change was anticipated.

document_sections.heading: Investigating injuries to the cervical spine
document_sections.content: The committee prioritised sensitivity to avoid missing serious cervical injuries and subsequent disability. Diagnostic evidence was limited because studies did not report the proportion with confirmed head injury, but suggested poorer X-ray sensitivity than CT for people 16 and over. On that evidence and current practice, initial cervical X-rays were not favoured for this age group; CT remained consistent with practice. MRI evidence was limited; MRI shows bony injury less accurately, takes longer and may require sedation in younger people, so it was retained as additional imaging in selected circumstances rather than usual initial imaging. For people under 16, limited evidence and radiation-associated cancer concerns supported avoiding major changes. Adult cervical CT had already largely replaced X-rays when risk was at least medium, so no practice change was expected.

document_sections.heading: Admission and observation
document_sections.content: Limited cohort evidence on intracranial injury suggested larger overall effect sizes for decision rules than isolated risk factors, but rule studies were retrospective; the committee therefore could not recommend a specific new rule. Across studies, including 1 in people under 16, GCS 13 or 14 was associated with poorer outcomes than GCS 15, already an admission indication. CT features such as subdural or epidural haemorrhage dimensions, midline shift and mass effect sometimes had larger effect sizes than other factors, but varying thresholds prevented identification of an ideal cut-off. Older-age thresholds might signal worse outcomes, but age or frailty alone should not determine admission, especially given possible hospital-acquired infection. Prospective validation of admission rules for GCS 13, 14 or 15 and CT-confirmed injury was proposed. Case series of babies and children with isolated skull fracture, with study-specific age limits, suggested low risks of death, neurosurgery, critical care, unplanned admission and delayed intracranial injury, but slightly higher rates of presenting seizure and evaluation for non-accidental injury. The committee judged simple linear non-displaced fractures unlikely to be clinically important and considered discharge after shared decisions safe for people under 16 with normal neurological status and no safeguarding concern. There was no direct adult evidence; indirect cohort evidence suggested lower deterioration risk with simple fracture than with complex fracture, 1 to 2 bleeds, bleeds less than 5 mm in diameter, no or minimal mass effect, significant midline shift, high- or mixed-density lesion, or cerebellar or brain stem injury. The studied simple-fracture group included both isolated and non-isolated injuries. The committee considered discharge after shared decisions safe for otherwise suitable people 16 and over with isolated fracture, except those taking anticoagulants or antiplatelets. Evidence on admission after normal imaging or without early-imaging indication among medication users was limited. Non-randomised anticoagulant studies, including at least 1 propensity-matched study of about 70,000 people, suggested no clinically important difference in delayed bleeding versus no anticoagulant use. The committee found medication status alone insufficient for admission after negative CT; admission itself can harm vulnerable people and delayed bleeds are usually not clinically important. Antiplatelet comparisons were still more limited, without large studies and with differences of only 1 to 2 events per study; antiplatelet status alone likewise did not justify admission after negative CT or when CT was not indicated. No evidence specifically examined disposition for concussion symptoms with normal imaging or no imaging indication. The committee considered most such patients safe for discharge without additional intervention unless standard admission criteria apply, while ensuring return precautions and support for persistent symptoms. Admission can worsen a person's condition through unfamiliar noise or infection risk. Fewer isolated-fracture admissions were expected; no significant change was proposed for medication users or concussion symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Early diagnosis of hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: More severe injury raises hypopituitarism risk, but even mild injury can cause it; onset can be immediate or delayed by weeks or months, and diverse symptoms complicate diagnosis. The committee supplemented a small amount of observational cohort evidence with expertise. The causal process is not fully understood, screening varies, and emergency department CT does not commonly identify the condition. Familiarity and suspicion may influence detection. Acute injury stimulates cortisol, potentially making emergency testing for hypoadrenalism difficult to interpret. The committee therefore favoured investigation in admitted people with clinical or biochemical indications such as hypotension or hyponatraemia, allowing specialist referral. Because evidence on testing time was absent, it requested research. Greater inpatient investigation and earlier specialist referral may result.

document_sections.heading: Discharge and follow up
document_sections.content: Studies involving anticoagulant or antiplatelet users reported some pre-existing cognitive impairment, including dementia, Parkinson's disease or stroke, but did not assess its effect on outcomes. Other examples across ages include developmental delay, Down's syndrome, cerebral palsy, fetal alcohol syndrome, learning disability, autism spectrum disorder and conditions altering sensation; adult examples also include depression, dementia and medication effects. The committee considered such people less likely to recognise or report early warning signs of delayed intracranial bleeding, such as severe headache, drowsiness or vomiting. Current practice may use a short overnight observation admission if home supervision is unavailable. Discharged people with prior cognitive impairment and those returning to custody need appropriate observation, and patients and carers need written head-injury advice. A small increase in overnight admissions without home supervision was possible, potentially improving outcomes after deterioration and reducing longer-term care costs.

document_sections.heading: Follow up
document_sections.content: Head-injury causes and contributing factors may need investigation or management. Persistent physical, sensory, motor, cognitive, emotional or hormonal problems, including hypopituitarism, can occur even without admission or despite normal initial imaging. People should know how to seek support, and clinicians should arrange appropriate outpatient referral; some also need services to reduce further injury risk. More primary-care referrals to outpatient clinics may occur for people initially discharged or without an abnormal scan, potentially enabling earlier treatment and prevention.

document_sections.heading: Investigations for hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: The committee considered additional endocrine evaluation appropriate to consider after discharge if compatible symptoms persist or recovery is unexpected. Symptoms may be non-specific or have another cause. In people under 16, delayed manifestations can include slow growth, tiredness and late puberty; suspected hypopituitarism in this age group warrants urgent referral to a paediatric endocrinologist. Awareness may increase primary-care testing and accelerate appropriate referral.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: In the UK, head injury is a major cause of death and disability from ages 1 to 40. Each year, over 1 million people in England and Wales attend emergency departments after recent head injury; between 33% and 50% are under 15. About 200,000 are admitted annually, of whom about 40,000 have evidence of traumatic brain injury. Most recover without specific or specialist intervention, but others develop lasting disability or die from brain or other injuries. An increasing share of presentations involves people over 65, and many injuries follow low-level falls, sometimes during acute illness. Mortality among emergency department attenders may be as low as 0.2%. Of injured people, 95% present with GCS 13 or more; most deaths occur among the moderate GCS 9 to 12 and severe GCS 8 or less groups, which together account for only 5% of attenders. Emergency departments must therefore identify the small group at risk of major acute intracranial complications. Abuse is estimated to cause head injury in 25% to 30% of hospitalised children under 2. The update addresses safeguarding terminology, transport to neuroscience care, head and cervical imaging indications and timing—including anticoagulants and circulating brain injury biomarkers—tranexamic acid, pituitary injury and discharge information.
